features.title: Incognito chats
features.summary: An incognito chat is a temporary conversation that is not saved to your chat history or to Claude's memory.
features.when: Use one for a one-off question you do not want shaping future answers or cluttering your history. If you want to keep the chat but skip memory, turn off Memory for that chat instead.
features.replaces: Deleting a chat afterwards and then pruning what it added to memory.

docs.title: Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context

features.example:
I am preparing for a difficult conversation with a colleague about missed handoffs during on-call.

Play the colleague. Push back the way a defensive but reasonable engineer would. After five exchanges, stop and tell me which of my phrasings made things worse and how to say them better.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Start a new chat outside of a project.
  2. Click the ghost icon in the upper right corner of the screen.
  3. Check for the black border and the Incognito chat label in the upper left corner.
  4. Have your conversation, and copy out anything you need to keep.
  5. Click the x in the upper right corner to close it.

Example

I am preparing for a difficult conversation with a colleague about missed handoffs during on-call.

Play the colleague. Push back the way a defensive but reasonable engineer would. After five exchanges, stop and tell me which of my phrasings made things worse and how to say them better.

At work

  • Practice and personal topics. Rehearse a hard conversation or think through a career question without it appearing in memory or in your monthly recap.
  • Clean-slate answers. An incognito chat does not use Claude's existing memory, so it is a quick way to see how Claude answers without your saved context.
  • Unrelated side quests. Keep a one-off question about a hobby from influencing work chats.

Pitfalls

  • Incognito is not the same as deleted. Chats are retained for 30 days by default, or longer under an organization's data retention setting.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans, incognito chats are included in organizational data exports available to Owners.
  • Claude can still access your profile information, such as personal preferences, in an incognito chat.
  • An incognito chat cannot be converted to a regular chat, and once closed it cannot be reopened.
  • It is only available outside projects. Inside a project, turn off Memory in the + menu before your first message.
  • If you have the new Claude experience, incognito chats open in the previous chat experience, so Claude cannot create files or run code in them.

features.title: Memory
features.summary: Memory lets Claude save context from your chats as individual topics and carry it into new conversations and cloud Cowork tasks.
features.when: Rely on memory for stable facts about you, such as your role, your stack, the people you work with and how you like things written. Use a project when the context is a body of documents.
features.replaces: Opening every chat with the same paragraph about who you are, what you work on and how you want answers formatted.

docs.title: Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context

features.example:
Remember this about how I work:
- I am a software engineer on a storage infrastructure team. Most of my code is Go and Python, and I work in VS Code.
- Our tickets live in Jira and our design docs in Confluence.
- For status updates, write three short sections named Done, Next and Risks.
- When you review code, lead with correctness problems and keep style notes to a short list at the end.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Go to Settings > Your Claude (or Settings > Memory in the older Settings layout) and check that Generate memory from chats is on.
  2. In a chat, tell Claude to "remember this" along with the facts you want kept.
  3. Select Manage next to Your memory to see what is saved under Topics. Open a topic to edit or delete it.
  4. Start a new chat and ask for something that depends on those facts.
  5. For a chat that should not touch memory, click + in the message box and turn off Memory before you send the first message.

Example

Remember this about how I work:
- I am a software engineer on a storage infrastructure team. Most of my code is Go and Python, and I work in VS Code.
- Our tickets live in Jira and our design docs in Confluence.
- For status updates, write three short sections named Done, Next and Risks.
- When you review code, lead with correctness problems and keep style notes to a short list at the end.

At work

  • Consistent output without preamble. Status reports and review comments come back in your format from the first message.
  • One memory across chat and Cowork. What Claude learns in chat is available to Cowork tasks that run in the cloud, and the reverse.

Pitfalls

  • By default Claude does not store sensitive topics such as health or politics unless you turn on Include sensitive topics in memory. Some information, such as government ID and financial account numbers, is never saved.
  • Deleting a conversation does not remove memory entries generated from it. Delete the memory itself.
  • Reset memory permanently deletes all memories, including project memories.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans, owners control whether memory is available.

features.title: Projects
features.summary: A project is a self-contained workspace with its own chats, uploaded knowledge and standing instructions.
features.when: Reach for a project when you keep pasting the same design doc, runbook or style rules into fresh chats. Set it up once and every chat in it starts with that background.
features.replaces: Re-uploading the same files and retyping the same ground rules at the top of every conversation.

docs.title: How can I create and manage projects?

features.example:
This project covers the replication service for our block storage product.

Treat the uploaded design doc, runbook and API reference as the source of truth. Name the file you relied on for each claim. If the files do not answer a question, say so instead of guessing.

When I ask for a write-up, use short paragraphs and end with open questions.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open claude.ai/projects and click + New Project. Give it a name and description.
  2. On the project page, click + in the project knowledge area and upload the documents, text files or code you keep referring to.
  3. Click Set project instructions, say how Claude should behave in this project, and click Save instructions.
  4. Start a chat inside the project and ask about the uploaded files.

Example

This project covers the replication service for our block storage product.

Treat the uploaded design doc, runbook and API reference as the source of truth. Name the file you relied on for each claim. If the files do not answer a question, say so instead of guessing.

When I ask for a write-up, use short paragraphs and end with open questions.

At work

  • One project per service. With the design doc and runbook in project knowledge, "what does the failover path do?" is answered from your documents.
  • Onboarding. On Team and Enterprise plans you can share a project with Can view or Can edit access, so a new teammate can question the same knowledge base.
  • Cheaper repeat questions. Project content is cached, so reusing the same documents counts less against your usage limits than uploading them each time.

Pitfalls

  • Context is not shared across chats in a project unless it is in the project knowledge base.
  • Claude does not see the project name or description.
  • Free accounts can create at most five projects, and the expanded RAG knowledge capacity is for paid plans.
  • Each project has its own memory. Turn off Use account memory on the project page to keep it fully separate.
  • A new version of projects is rolling out in beta, starting with Claude Code, so yours may look different.

features.title: Search past chats
features.summary: Chat search lets you ask Claude to find and reference what you discussed in previous conversations.
features.when: Use it when you know you worked something out with Claude before and want to continue from there, instead of scrolling the sidebar or explaining it again.
features.replaces: Hunting through old chats for the one where you settled a design question, then copy-pasting the relevant part.

docs.title: Use Claude's chat search and memory to build on previous context

features.example:
Find our earlier conversation about the snapshot retention policy for the backup service.

Summarize what we decided, list the open questions we left, and then draft the "Decision" section of the design doc from it. Link the chats you used.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open a new chat. Once the feature has rolled out to your account it is on by default.
  2. Ask naturally, for example "What did we discuss about [topic]?" or "Let's continue where we left off with [project]."
  3. Watch for the tool call in the chat. That is Claude searching your previous conversations.
  4. Follow the citations in the answer back to the original chats to confirm the details.

Example

Find our earlier conversation about the snapshot retention policy for the backup service.

Summarize what we decided, list the open questions we left, and then draft the "Decision" section of the design doc from it. Link the chats you used.

At work

  • Picking up a design thread. Resume a multi-day discussion without re-explaining the constraints you already worked through.
  • Writing from your own history. Turn several past debugging chats into one incident write-up or a runbook entry, with links to the conversations it came from.
  • Less repetition, less usage. The usage best-practice guide points out that letting Claude pull prior context saves you from providing the same information repeatedly.

Pitfalls

  • Searching past chats is for paid plans, per the docs.
  • Scope is limited. From a chat outside projects Claude searches all chats outside projects. Inside a project it searches only that project's conversations.
  • Incognito chats are never searched, and a chat started with memory turned off does not search your past chats.
  • You can switch it off with the Search and reference chats toggle in Settings > Your Claude (or Settings > Memory in the older Settings layout).
  • It is not available if your organization uses customer-managed encryption keys on an Enterprise plan.
  • Citations include an option to delete the referenced conversation. Deleting is separate from memory, which keeps entries generated from deleted chats.

features.title: Claude Duet
features.summary: Claude Duet is a research preview of Claude that you message the way you would message a person, and that works in your connected apps from its own computer in the cloud.
features.when: Consider it for personal admin and follow-ups you want handled in the background, with approval before anything is sent, paid, signed or deleted. It is not available on Team or Enterprise plans yet.
features.replaces: Manually triaging your inbox and calendar each morning and chasing threads that have gone quiet.
features.example:
Pull together a brief on this company before my 2 pm meeting.

Use my email and calendar to find who I am meeting and what we last discussed. Add recent public news about them. Keep it to one page and tell me which email or file each fact came from.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Go to the Claude Duet product page and select Join the waitlist.
  2. Enter your name and the email address on your Claude account, your plan and your phone type, then select Submit.
  3. When the invitation email arrives, open it on your phone and follow the setup steps for iPhone or Android. Your memory, skills and connectors are already there.
  4. Send a first request, typed or as a voice message, and watch the Tasks tab for anything that needs your input.

Example

Pull together a brief on this company before my 2 pm meeting.

Use my email and calendar to find who I am meeting and what we last discussed. Add recent public news about them. Keep it to one page and tell me which email or file each fact came from.

At work

  • Morning brief. Each morning it looks across your email and calendar, picks what most needs attention, and can draft replies for you to review.
  • Larger jobs. Bigger results, such as a research brief or a slide deck, appear in the Make tab.
  • Sites without a connector. It uses its own browser in the cloud.

Pitfalls

  • It is a research preview, available through a waitlist to Pro, Max and Ultra plans in the US. It is not available on Team or Enterprise plans yet.
  • You cannot choose a model, watch it work in its browser or take over the browser.
  • It checks your accounts at set intervals, so something urgent can arrive between checks.
  • It cannot see the files on your computer or all of your projects, and Microsoft 365 is not available yet.
  • Content it reads can contain instructions meant to mislead it, so review drafts and approval requests.

features.title: Connectors
features.summary: Connectors let Claude access your apps and services, retrieve your data and take actions in them, using the permissions you already have there.
features.when: Connect a service when you keep copying its content into Claude or carrying Claude's output back to it. One connection replaces every future copy and paste for that tool.
features.replaces: Exporting tickets, emails and documents by hand so Claude can read them, then re-entering the result in the source system.

docs.title: Use connectors to extend Claude's capabilities

features.example:
Summarize the open issues assigned to me, grouped by epic.

For each one give the key, a one-line status, and what is blocking it. Flag anything untouched for more than two weeks. Then draft a comment for the three stalest issues asking the reporter whether it is still needed. Show me the drafts before posting anything.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Go to Customize > Connectors, select Discover, and search for a service you use.
  2. Open its page, select Connect to Claude, sign in to the service and approve the access it asks for.
  3. In a chat, select + in the message box, then Connectors, and make sure the connector's toggle is on.
  4. Ask for something the service holds. When Claude asks to use a tool, select Allow once or Always allow.

Example

Summarize the open issues assigned to me, grouped by epic.

For each one give the key, a one-line status, and what is blocking it. Flag anything untouched for more than two weeks. Then draft a comment for the three stalest issues asking the reporter whether it is still needed. Show me the drafts before posting anything.

At work

  • Standup and status prep. Claude reads your tracker and calendar directly, so a weekly status draft starts from real data instead of memory.
  • Acting, not only reading. The docs' own example is asking Claude to "Create a new issue for the login bug" after connecting an issue tracker.
  • Same connectors everywhere. Connectors you add in claude.ai are available in Claude Code when you sign in with your Claude account.

Pitfalls

  • Connecting grants Claude permission to access and potentially modify data based on your account permissions. Only connect services you trust and need.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner must add the connector for the organization before members can connect.
  • Verification of a directory connector is not a security audit.
  • Many active connectors take up room in the conversation. With 10 or more, the docs suggest switching Tool access from Auto to On demand.
  • Turning a toggle off in a chat does not sign Claude out. Use Disconnect for that.

features.title: Create a custom skill
features.summary: A custom skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions, and optionally scripts and reference files, that you write once and upload so Claude follows your process.
features.when: Write one when you find yourself correcting Claude with the same instructions, such as a report format, a review checklist or a multi-step procedure. For a one-off task, just describe it in the conversation.
features.replaces: Keeping a personal prompt file and pasting from it whenever the task comes up.
features.example:
---
name: incident-writeup
description: Write a post-incident review in our team format. Use when asked for an incident write-up, postmortem or PIR.
---

# Incident write-up

1. Build a timeline in UTC from the material provided. Mark gaps instead of guessing.
2. Write these sections in order: Summary, Customer impact, Timeline, Root cause, Action items.
3. Keep the Summary under 100 words and refer to roles, not names.
4. Give every action item an owner role and a due date.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Create a folder named after the skill, for example incident-writeup, containing a SKILL.md that starts with name and description frontmatter.
  2. From the parent folder run zip -r incident-writeup.zip incident-writeup/ so the folder is the top level of the archive.
  3. Go to Customize > Skills, click the + button, then + Create skill, select Upload a skill and upload the ZIP.
  4. Turn the skill on and send a prompt that should trigger it.
  5. If Claude does not load it when expected, revise the description.

Example

---
name: incident-writeup
description: Write a post-incident review in our team format. Use when asked for an incident write-up, postmortem or PIR.
---

# Incident write-up

1. Build a timeline in UTC from the material provided. Mark gaps instead of guessing.
2. Write these sections in order: Summary, Customer impact, Timeline, Root cause, Action items.
3. Keep the Summary under 100 words and refer to roles, not names.
4. Give every action item an owner role and a due date.

At work

  • Teaching tool conventions. A skill can tell Claude which project new issues go in and which labels and template to use in your issue tracker.
  • Sharing. On Team and Enterprise plans you can share a skill with colleagues or use Publish to org, if an owner has enabled it.

Pitfalls

  • The directory name must match the name field, which allows lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only. A SKILL.md at the root of the ZIP is not recognized.
  • Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and move reference material to separate files.
  • Do not put API keys or passwords anywhere in a skill. Everyone you share it with receives its files.
  • A skill cannot reach an outside service itself. Live data needs a connector.

features.title: Custom connectors (remote MCP)
features.summary: A custom connector links Claude to any remote MCP server by its URL, including one you build for an internal tool.
features.when: Use one when the service you need is not in the Connectors Directory, or when you want Claude to reach an internal system through an MCP server your team hosts.
features.replaces: Writing one-off scripts to dump internal data into files that you then upload to Claude.

docs.title: Get started with custom connectors using remote MCP
Add a connector that isn't in the directory

features.example:
Name:            Build Farm
MCP server URL:  https://mcp.example.com/mcp
Authentication:  Sign in now            (or "Sign in when needed" or "No sign-in")
OAuth client:    Use Claude's published identity
Request headers: only for a fixed credential such as an API key, for example
                 x-api-key = the key exactly as your server expects it, marked Required
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Go to Customize > Connectors. Select Add, then Add custom connector. On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner does this in Organization settings > Connectors instead.
  2. Enter a name and the remote MCP server URL, then click Continue.
  3. Keep the authentication options marked Detected unless the server's documentation says otherwise, then click Add.
  4. If the connector shows Connect, click it and sign in.
  5. In a chat, click +, select Connectors, and turn the connector on for that conversation.

Example

Name:            Build Farm
MCP server URL:  https://mcp.example.com/mcp
Authentication:  Sign in now            (or "Sign in when needed" or "No sign-in")
OAuth client:    Use Claude's published identity
Request headers: only for a fixed credential such as an API key, for example
                 x-api-key = the key exactly as your server expects it, marked Required

At work

  • Internal systems. Put an MCP server in front of your build farm, test results or capacity database and ask questions about them from chat, Cowork or Claude Desktop.
  • Team-wide access. An Owner adds the connector once and each member clicks Connect to authenticate.
  • Service accounts. Request headers suit services where everyone shares one credential, such as an internal tool.

Pitfalls

  • Claude connects from Anthropic's cloud, not from your machine, on every client. A server behind a VPN or firewall will not connect unless you allowlist Anthropic's IP ranges or use an MCP tunnel.
  • Connect only to servers you trust and review the permission scopes requested.
  • Malicious servers may include hidden instructions. Only click Always allow for trusted servers.
  • You cannot change authentication settings after adding. Remove the connector and add it again.
  • Request header authentication is in beta for a limited set of organizations, and you can add up to four headers.
  • Free accounts are limited to one custom connector.

features.title: Google Workspace connectors
features.summary: The Google Workspace connectors link Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive to Claude, and let it edit Google Docs, Sheets and Slides live in a pane beside the chat.
features.when: Use them when the answer lives in your mail, calendar or Drive, or when you want Claude to edit a Google file in place instead of producing a download.
features.replaces: Pasting email threads and document text into chat, and copying Claude's edits back into the Google file.
features.example:
Look at my calendar for next week and the email threads with each meeting's attendees from the last 14 days.

For every meeting I am hosting, give me: the open questions from the threads and a three-line agenda. Then make a Google doc called "Week prep" with one section per meeting.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Connect Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive from Customize > Connectors and authenticate with your Google account.
  2. In a chat, click the plus sign, hover over Connectors and toggle on the ones you need, including the separate Docs, Sheets and Slides connectors for live editing.
  3. Ask a question that needs your mail, calendar or Drive. By default Claude asks for approval before actions such as sending email or sharing files.
  4. To edit live, paste a Google Docs, Sheets or Slides link, or ask for a Google file by name.

Example

Look at my calendar for next week and the email threads with each meeting's attendees from the last 14 days.

For every meeting I am hosting, give me: the open questions from the threads and a three-line agenda. Then make a Google doc called "Week prep" with one section per meeting.

At work

  • Meeting prep. Claude cites which emails, calendar events and documents it used, with links to the originals when available.
  • Scheduling. The Calendar connector can find mutual availability across attendees and create, update or delete events.
  • Editing in place. You and Claude can work in the same Google file at the same time.

Pitfalls

  • Asking for a generic "doc" or "deck" without naming Google creates a local file instead.
  • Claude extracts text only from Drive files, and sees Gmail attachment metadata but not content.
  • Claude cannot add charts to Google Slides, and Slides edits may not appear live in the pane.
  • The live pane works on Claude on the web in Chrome, and on Claude Desktop with the built-in browser turned on. Otherwise select Open in Google on the file card.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner must enable the connectors first.

features.title: Interactive connectors
features.summary: Some connectors can display live, interactive apps inside a Claude conversation, such as a task board or analytics dashboard, instead of a text-only reply.
features.when: Use one when you want to see and adjust the real thing while you talk about it, rather than read a description and switch tabs to act on it.
features.replaces: Asking Claude for a summary, then opening the tool in another tab to make the change yourself.
features.example:
Draft a Slack message for the #storage-oncall channel summarizing last night's incident:
- what paged, when, and for how long
- customer impact in one sentence
- the mitigation we applied
- the follow-up ticket link placeholder

Keep it under 120 words. Show me the draft so I can edit it before it is sent.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open the Connectors Directory and look for connectors marked with the Interactive badge.
  2. Connect and authenticate with one. No additional setup is needed.
  3. Start a conversation and ask about something that connector handles. The interactive view appears automatically when relevant.
  4. Work in the view directly, for example filter data or check off a task, or ask Claude to make the change.

Example

Draft a Slack message for the #storage-oncall channel summarizing last night's incident:
- what paged, when, and for how long
- customer impact in one sentence
- the mitigation we applied
- the follow-up ticket link placeholder

Keep it under 120 words. Show me the draft so I can edit it before it is sent.

At work

  • Review before sending. Inline cards suit single actions such as a message draft ready to send.
  • Boards and dashboards in the chat. Ask about project status and the task board opens in the conversation, where you can check off tasks.
  • Keep a view open. The side panel keeps the connector open beside your chat so you can watch it update, and supported connectors can be pinned to your sidebar.

Pitfalls

  • What you see varies by connector. Each developer chooses which views and actions to support, and Claude can only take actions the developer has made available.
  • The side panel, full-site views and pinning are rolling out on the web and in Claude Desktop to accounts with the new Claude experience. They are not on Claude Mobile yet.
  • Pins are saved per browser, so a pin added on the web does not appear in Claude Desktop.
  • Purchases through a connector's in-chat views are not supported.
  • Team and Enterprise owners can disable the tool calls that render interactive views. The connector's text-based tools keep working.

features.title: Microsoft 365 connector
features.summary: The Microsoft 365 connector lets Claude search, analyze and act on Outlook email and calendar and OneDrive files, plus SharePoint and Teams with a work or school account.
features.when: Use it when the context you need is spread across Outlook threads, SharePoint libraries and Teams channels, and you want one question to search all of them.
features.replaces: Searching Outlook, SharePoint and Teams separately and stitching the results together by hand.
features.example:
Search the Engineering team site in SharePoint for architecture documents about the metadata service, and find emails from the last two weeks about its migration.

Summarize the current plan, list decisions and who made them, and point out where the documents and the emails disagree. Draft a reply to the latest email in the thread with my questions, but don't send it.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Go to Customize > Connectors and find Microsoft 365 in the list.
  2. Click Add and choose Work or school account if asked, then sign in with that account. An admin must have set the connector up first.
  3. In a chat, click the + button, hover over Connectors and toggle Microsoft 365 on.
  4. Ask a question that names where to look, such as a SharePoint site, a date range or a sender.

Example

Search the Engineering team site in SharePoint for architecture documents about the metadata service, and find emails from the last two weeks about its migration.

Summarize the current plan, list decisions and who made them, and point out where the documents and the emails disagree. Draft a reply to the latest email in the thread with my questions, but don't send it.

At work

  • Catching up on a thread. Ask for an email thread summary with key points and decisions.
  • Finding the spec. Claude searches SharePoint sites, document libraries and shared OneDrive folders you can already access.
  • Follow-through. If your admin has enabled write tools, Claude can draft and send email, manage calendar events, create and update files, and send Teams messages.

Pitfalls

  • Work or school accounts need admin setup, including a one-time consent by a Microsoft Entra Global Administrator.
  • Without write tools the integration is read-only. By default Claude asks you to confirm before it sends or changes something.
  • Attachments are not supported in write tools, so Claude cannot send, forward or draft emails with attachments.
  • Only Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF and plain-text formats can be read. OneNote is not supported.
  • You cannot scope the connector to specific SharePoint sites. It searches everything you have permission to access.
  • A personal account does not include SharePoint or Teams.

features.title: Plugins in Claude
features.summary: A plugin packages skills, MCP connectors, commands and agents so you can add them to Claude as one unit that follows your account across chat, Cowork and Claude Code.
features.when: Add a plugin when you want a ready-made setup for a role or tool, or want your team's skills and connectors installed and shared together. Add a single skill or connector on its own when that is all you need.
features.replaces: Installing and configuring each skill and connector separately on every surface you use.
features.example:
/engineering:standup

Use my calendar and issue tracker connectors. Cover yesterday, today and blockers, and keep it under 120 words so I can paste it into the team channel.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open Customize > Plugins and select Discover.
  2. Select a plugin to read what it contains, then select Add.
  3. Open the plugin's Connectors tab and connect any connector that shows Not connected or Not added.
  4. In a chat, type / in the message box, type the plugin's name to narrow the list, and select a skill.
  5. If it does not help, turn it off with its Disable plugin toggle or select Remove from its menu.

Example

In Cowork, run a plugin's command by name (these names are placeholders):

/engineering:standup

Use my calendar and issue tracker connectors. Cover yesterday, today and blockers, and keep it under 120 words so I can paste it into the team channel.

At work

  • Role setups. Anthropic-built plugins cover functions including engineering, data analysis and operations, each with the relevant skills and connectors.
  • Team standard. Use Add > Add marketplace with a Git repository of your team's plugins.
  • One install, three surfaces. A plugin added in claude.ai loads into your Cowork tasks and syncs to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account.

Pitfalls

  • Adding a plugin does not add a connector or sign you in to anything. Skills that use a connector cannot reach the service until it shows Connected.
  • Chat only uses a plugin's skills, commands and connectors. Agents and hooks run in Cowork and Claude Code.
  • Anthropic's review covers plugins listed in the directory, not ones you add from a marketplace URL or upload yourself. Add those only from sources you trust.
  • Plugins may include local MCP servers that run on your computer with the same permissions as any other program you run.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner controls which sources you see. Required plugins cannot be turned off.

features.title: Skills in Claude
features.summary: Skills are folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads only when a task calls for them, so it does that task the same way every time.
features.when: Turn on a skill when you want Claude to follow a specific procedure for a recurring task. Use a project for background knowledge that should always be loaded in its chats.
features.replaces: Pasting the same checklist or template into a chat every time you ask for that kind of output.
features.example:
Create a PowerPoint presentation for Thursday's architecture review of the tiering service.

Six slides: problem, current design, proposed design, migration plan, risks, decisions needed. Use the attached design doc as the only source. Put the detail in speaker notes and keep each slide to four bullets or fewer.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Make sure Code execution and file creation is on under Settings > Capabilities. Skills run in Claude's code sandbox.
  2. Open Customize > Skills. Your skills lists what you have and Discover lists skills you can add.
  3. Select Turn on on a skill's row, or open the skill and use the switch at the top of its page.
  4. In a chat, describe your task. Claude loads a turned-on skill when the task matches its description.
  5. To pick one yourself, type / in the message box and select the skill.

Example

Create a PowerPoint presentation for Thursday's architecture review of the tiering service.

Six slides: problem, current design, proposed design, migration plan, risks, decisions needed. Use the attached design doc as the only source. Put the detail in speaker notes and keep each slide to four bullets or fewer.

At work

  • Documents that come out right. The Anthropic skills for Excel, Word, PowerPoint and PDF are available to all users and are invoked automatically.
  • Team conventions. Custom skills can create tasks in tools such as JIRA following team conventions, or structure meeting notes in a company format.
  • Everywhere you work. Enabled skills are also available in the Claude add-ins for Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook, and sync to Claude Code.

Pitfalls

  • A skill's description is the only part Claude sees before deciding to use it. If Claude is not using a skill, check that it is toggled on and be explicit, for example "Use my brand guidelines skill to...".
  • Skills that someone shares with you or that you upload are not reviewed by Anthropic. Read the SKILL.md and bundled files before turning one on.
  • If skills are greyed out, code execution may be disabled for you or your organization.

features.title: Model, effort and thinking settings
features.summary: The model menu next to the send button sets which Claude model you chat with, how much effort it puts into each response, and whether it shows its thinking.
features.when: Raise effort or turn on thinking for multi-step technical problems, detailed document analysis and project planning. Leave the defaults, or go lower, for everyday questions.
features.replaces: Re-asking the same hard question several times hoping for a more careful answer.

docs.title: Change the model, effort, and thinking settings
When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research?

features.example:
Here is our lease-based leader election code and the failure report from last night.

Work through every interleaving in which two nodes could both believe they hold the lease, given clock drift of up to 500 ms and a network partition during renewal. For each one, say whether the code allows it and which line is responsible. Then propose the smallest fix.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Click the model name next to the send button.
  2. Click Effort and choose a level. The recommended level for each model is marked Default.
  3. On models that offer it, mouse over Effort and switch the Thinking (or Extended) toggle on or off.
  4. Send a hard problem, then click the expandable Thinking section above the reply to see how Claude approached it.

Example

Here is our lease-based leader election code and the failure report from last night.

Work through every interleaving in which two nodes could both believe they hold the lease, given clock drift of up to 500 ms and a network partition during renewal. For each one, say whether the code allows it and which line is responsible. Then propose the smallest fix.

At work

  • Hard technical problems. Higher effort means more thorough responses, which the docs recommend for multi-step technical problems and detailed document analysis.
  • Stretching your usage. The docs say Low and Medium work well for routine tasks and stretch your usage further.
  • Checking the reasoning. Reading the thinking summary helps you verify how Claude reached its conclusion before you rely on it.

Pitfalls

  • Higher effort takes longer and uses more tokens, so you reach usage limits faster.
  • Effort and thinking are separate settings. Effort controls how thorough every response is. The toggle controls whether Claude works through its reasoning in an expandable section first.
  • On some models thinking is always on and the toggle does not appear. To make Claude think less on these, choose a lower effort level.
  • The effort selector is only available on some models, and on Enterprise plans an administrator may have turned off a model or effort level for your role.
  • Changes apply from Claude's next response, not retroactively.

features.title: Research
features.summary: Research makes Claude investigate a question in depth, running many searches that build on each other across the web and your connected tools, then writing a cited report.
features.when: Use it for comprehensive information gathering that needs five or more lookups, such as a vendor comparison or a technology survey. For a quick fact, plain web search is enough.
features.replaces: An afternoon of opening tabs, skimming sources and pasting notes into a comparison document.

docs.title: When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research?

features.example:
Use the research tool to compare erasure coding and three-way replication for an object store serving mostly cold data.

Cover: storage overhead, rebuild time after a disk failure, read latency, and operational complexity.
Prefer vendor engineering blogs, conference papers and official documentation from the last three years.
Pull relevant context from our design docs in Google Docs.
End with a one-page recommendation and a table of sources.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Make sure web search is turned on. Research does not work without it.
  2. Click the + button at the bottom left of the chat box, then Research. A blue indicator appears at the bottom of the chat window.
  3. Ask your question and say what the report should cover.
  4. Read the report and open the citations for anything you will act on.
  5. Click the indicator again to turn research off.

Example

Use the research tool to compare erasure coding and three-way replication for an object store serving mostly cold data.

Cover: storage overhead, rebuild time after a disk failure, read latency, and operational complexity.
Prefer vendor engineering blogs, conference papers and official documentation from the last three years.
Pull relevant context from our design docs in Google Docs.
End with a one-page recommendation and a table of sources.

At work

  • Design doc background. Get a cited survey of prior art before you write the "alternatives considered" section.
  • Internal plus external. On the web or Claude Desktop, research also searches connectors you have turned on for the chat, such as Google Workspace.
  • Refreshing stale pages. The docs give updating outdated internal documents with information from the web as a fit.

Pitfalls

  • Research is for paid plans.
  • Started from Claude Mobile, research only searches the web and skips your connectors with no error or warning.
  • It cannot use tools from local MCP servers configured in Claude Desktop.
  • During research Claude uses connector tools automatically, without asking for approval each time.
  • It can use up your usage limits faster than normal chats.
  • Research runs on its own model no matter which model you picked for the chat.
  • If Claude does not start researching, say "please use the research tool to..." in your prompt.

features.title: Web search and web fetch
features.summary: Web search lets Claude look things up on the live web and answer with citations, and web fetch lets it read a specific URL you give it.
features.when: Use it for current facts that one or two lookups can settle, such as a release note, an error message or a changelog entry. Use Research when the question needs a full report.
features.replaces: Switching to a browser, searching, reading three pages and carrying the answer back into the chat.

docs.title: When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research?

features.example:
Search the web. What changed in the latest stable Linux kernel release that affects NVMe over TCP?

Give me the three most relevant changes, each with a link to the primary source (kernel changelog or mailing list), and note anything that needs a configuration change on our side.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Click the + button in the lower left corner of the chat window.
  2. Click Web search. A checkmark appears next to it when it is on.
  3. Ask something that needs current information, or include "Search the web" in your prompt to make sure Claude searches.
  4. Paste a URL and ask about it. With web search on, Claude can retrieve that page directly (web fetch).
  5. Check the citations and source links in the answer.

Example

Search the web. What changed in the latest stable Linux kernel release that affects NVMe over TCP?

Give me the three most relevant changes, each with a link to the primary source (kernel changelog or mailing list), and note anything that needs a configuration change on our side.

At work

  • Debugging. Paste an unfamiliar error and ask Claude to search for known issues, with links to the tracker entries it found.
  • Reading a long page for you. Give Claude the URL of a release note or RFC and ask for the parts that affect your system.
  • Steering the search. The docs suggest it when you want to tell Claude roughly what to look for and let it run the searches and analyze the results.

Pitfalls

  • If you have the new Claude experience there is no web search toggle. Claude searches when it helps.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans an Owner or Primary Owner must first enable web search in Organization settings > Capabilities.
  • Web search and web fetch count toward your usage limits. Fetching a long article pulls the whole thing into the context window.
  • Website links occasionally do not work, and Claude may use your location, inferred from your IP address, for localized results.
  • Cross-check cited sources and use authoritative ones for important decisions.

features.title: Prompt design basics
features.summary: A short set of documented prompting habits that make Claude's answers more useful, starting with being clear and direct and giving the context a new colleague would need.
features.when: Apply these whenever a first answer comes back generic or misses the point. They cost a minute of typing and usually save several rounds of correction.
features.replaces: One-line prompts followed by a string of corrective follow-ups.
features.example:
<document>
<source>design-doc-tiering-v3.md</source>
<document_content>
[paste the design doc]
</document_content>
</document>

Review this design as a senior storage engineer. I need the five most important concerns, not a full audit.

First quote the passages that worry you inside <quotes> tags. Then give each concern as one sentence of risk plus the question I should ask the author. Write plain prose, because I will paste this into a comment thread.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Write the request as you would brief a newly hired contractor who has no context about you, your task or your organization.
  2. Use numbered steps when the order matters.
  3. Say why an instruction matters. Claude can generalize from the explanation.
  4. Wrap pasted material in descriptive XML tags, put long documents at the top and your question at the end.
  5. Apply the docs' key test. If a colleague with minimal context would be confused by the prompt, Claude will be too.

Example

<document>
<source>design-doc-tiering-v3.md</source>
<document_content>
[paste the design doc]
</document_content>
</document>

Review this design as a senior storage engineer. I need the five most important concerns, not a full audit.

First quote the passages that worry you inside <quotes> tags. Then give each concern as one sentence of risk plus the question I should ask the author. Write plain prose, because I will paste this into a comment thread.

At work

  • Code and design review. A one-sentence role focuses Claude's behavior and tone for the task.
  • Consistent write-ups. The docs call examples one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure. Include 3 to 5, wrapped in <example> tags.
  • Long documents. Asking Claude to quote the relevant parts first helps it focus on what matters and ignore the rest.

Pitfalls

  • If you want Claude to do more than the task strictly requires, ask for it explicitly.
  • Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do. "Write in flowing prose paragraphs" works better than "do not use markdown".
  • Make examples diverse, or Claude picks up unintended patterns.
  • The detailed guide is written for API users, so sections such as system prompts do not apply directly to the chat app.

features.title: Working within usage limits
features.summary: A set of documented habits for getting more work out of your plan's session and weekly usage limits.
features.when: Apply these when you keep hitting your limit mid-task, or before a long working session where running out would hurt.
features.replaces: Firing off many short follow-up messages and re-uploading the same files until the limit cuts you off.

docs.title: How do usage and length limits work?

features.example:
Context: Go 1.22 service, PostgreSQL 15, running on Kubernetes. Full handler and its test are pasted below.

In one reply, please:
1. Explain why TestRetryBackoff fails intermittently.
2. Give the smallest fix as a diff.
3. List any other place in this file with the same bug.
4. Suggest one extra test that would have caught it.

[paste handler.go and handler_test.go]
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open Settings > Usage and look at Current session and Weekly limits to see where you stand.
  2. Put documents you reference repeatedly into a project. Project content is cached and counts less when reused.
  3. Combine related questions into a single message with all the background up front.
  4. Lower the effort level for routine tasks, and turn off connected apps a conversation does not need.
  5. Start a new conversation when a long chat is close to your limit.

Example

Context: Go 1.22 service, PostgreSQL 15, running on Kubernetes. Full handler and its test are pasted below.

In one reply, please:
1. Explain why TestRetryBackoff fails intermittently.
2. Give the smallest fix as a diff.
3. List any other place in this file with the same bug.
4. Suggest one extra test that would have caught it.

[paste handler.go and handler_test.go]

At work

  • Code review and debugging. Give complete context about your environment in the first message and include entire relevant snippets.
  • Editing documents. Send the whole text for editing in one message rather than in pieces.
  • Pacing. The session limit resets five hours after your first message and the weekly limit at a fixed time assigned to your account.

Pitfalls

  • Usage across claude.ai, Claude Code and Claude Desktop counts toward the same limit.
  • Tools and connectors are token-intensive. Research, web search, file creation, higher effort and model choice all affect how fast you use your limit.
  • Project caches expire after a period of inactivity. Your first message after a long break counts that content in full again.
  • Long conversations that trigger automatic context management consume more of your limit.
  • Usage limits and length limits are different. Hitting a length limit means starting a new conversation, not waiting.

features.title: Quick entry on Mac
features.summary: Quick entry in Claude Desktop on Mac opens Claude from any app with a keyboard shortcut, and lets you attach a screenshot or an application window or dictate your message.
features.when: Use it when you are in the middle of something and want to ask about what is on your screen without switching windows, copying text or saving a screenshot first.
features.replaces: Taking a screenshot, finding the file, switching to Claude and dragging it into a new chat.

docs.title: Use quick entry with Claude Desktop on Mac

features.example: This is the output of the failing integration test run. Which assertion failed first, and what does the stack trace say about where the nil pointer comes from? Give me the two most likely causes and the command to rerun only that test with verbose logging.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open Claude Desktop on your Mac. In the quick entry prompt, check Turn on shortcut and click Continue.
  2. From any application, double-tap the Option key. A text box appears.
  3. Click and drag to select an area of the screen, or click an application window to attach its contents.
  4. Type your question and press Enter.
  5. Optional. Enable the voice shortcut, then press Caps Lock once to start dictating and again to stop.

Example

After double-tapping Option and clicking your terminal window:

This is the output of the failing integration test run. Which assertion failed first, and what does the stack trace say about where the nil pointer comes from? Give me the two most likely causes and the command to rerun only that test with verbose logging.

At work

  • Debugging in flow. The docs list sharing error messages or application windows directly with Claude for debugging assistance.
  • Reading dashboards and diagrams. Capture part of a monitoring graph or an architecture diagram and ask a question about it without leaving the page.
  • Hands-free notes. Dictate a thought with real-time transcription, review it, then send.

Pitfalls

  • Quick entry is only available on macOS. Claude Desktop must be running, though it can be in the background.
  • It needs macOS 12 or later, and voice dictation needs macOS 14 or later.
  • The voice shortcut is disabled by default because it takes over your Caps Lock key.
  • It requires macOS permissions for screen recording and accessibility, plus speech recognition for dictation. Review them in System Settings > Privacy & Security.
  • If double-tap Option conflicts with another app, change Quick access shortcut in Settings > Desktop app to Option + Space or a custom shortcut.

features.title: Voice mode
features.summary: Voice mode lets you have a full spoken conversation with Claude, speaking your prompts and hearing its replies, and switch between voice and text in the same chat.
features.when: Use it when your hands are busy or when thinking out loud is faster than typing, such as a commute or a walk between meetings. Use dictation instead when you only want speech turned into a typed prompt.
features.replaces: Waiting until you are back at a keyboard to work through an idea or catch up on your day.
features.example: Catch me up before standup. Check my calendar for today and summarize any email threads from the last day that mention the replication rollout. Then ask me three questions about what I got done yesterday and turn my answers into a short update I can read out.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. On mobile, tap the voice mode icon (the sound wave symbol next to the microphone icon) in the text input field. On the web or Claude Desktop, start a new chat and tap the sound wave symbol in the lower right corner.
  2. Choose a voice when prompted.
  3. Start talking. In the default hands-free mode Claude responds when you finish a thought.
  4. In a noisy place, switch to push-to-talk and hold the button while speaking.
  5. On the web and desktop, click Stop to leave voice mode. The transcript stays in your chat history.

Example

Catch me up before standup. Check my calendar for today and summarize any email threads from the last day that mention the replication rollout. Then ask me three questions about what I got done yesterday and turn my answers into a short update I can read out.

At work

  • Morning briefing. With connected tools such as Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Docs and Slack, Claude can catch you up on email or check your calendar before a meeting by voice.
  • Rehearsal. The docs list practicing for interviews or important conversations through natural dialogue.
  • Capturing ideas. Talk an idea through, then switch to text in the same conversation to paste code or a URL.

Pitfalls

  • Voice mode is a beta feature and is built to work best from your phone.
  • Voice conversations count toward your regular usage limits.
  • Hands-free mode works best in quiet environments.
  • Not every result can be shown on screen in voice mode, and using several tools at once can add a short delay.
  • Claude Fable is not currently available in voice mode.
  • In Claude Cowork and Claude Code, dictation is available but voice mode is not.

features.title: Artifacts
features.summary: An artifact is a finished piece of work, such as a document, deck, design, dashboard or small interactive tool, that opens beside the chat where you can edit, share and export it.
features.when: Ask for an artifact when the answer is something you will put in front of other people or come back to, rather than a reply you read once.
features.replaces: Copying chat output into a separate editor and reformatting it before anyone else can see it.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Build a small interactive tool as an artifact: a capacity calculator for a storage array.

Inputs: raw capacity in TB, RAID overhead percent, expected data reduction ratio, monthly growth percent.
Outputs: usable capacity today, effective capacity after data reduction, and the month we cross 80 percent full.
Chart projected usage over 24 months and update it when I change an input.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In Settings > Capabilities, check that Cloud code execution and file creation is on (it is called Create and edit files in the updated Settings layout).
  2. Ask for an artifact in any chat, or select Output in the message box and choose a template, or pick one in the Artifacts tab.
  3. Change it by asking Claude, or edit directly in an artifact made from a template. In a doc, highlight text, click Edit with Claude and type the change.
  4. In an artifact made from a template, click Export when it is ready. Everything you make is saved in the Artifacts tab.

Example

Build a small interactive tool as an artifact: a capacity calculator for a storage array.

Inputs: raw capacity in TB, RAID overhead percent, expected data reduction ratio, monthly growth percent.
Outputs: usable capacity today, effective capacity after data reduction, and the month we cross 80 percent full.
Chart projected usage over 24 months and update it when I change an input.

At work

  • Small internal tools. A calculator or a triage checklist is ready in one prompt and, on paid plans, shareable by link.
  • Trackers that keep state. On paid plans an artifact can store data between sessions, in personal or shared storage.
  • Live views of your tools. On paid plans an artifact can read from and write to apps you have connected to Claude. Each person who opens it connects their own apps.

Pitfalls

  • Artifacts start private to you until you share them.
  • Storage is limited to 20 MB per artifact and text only. Check whether an artifact uses shared storage before entering anything sensitive.
  • Connector tools that need approval for each action are not available to artifacts.
  • Only build on a published artifact from someone you trust.

features.title: Claude Data
features.summary: Claude Data turns plain-language questions about your company's data into dashboards, data stories, narrated short videos and written analyses, with Claude writing the SQL.
features.when: Use it for quick, exploratory questions against a connected data warehouse or app, where you want a chart whose query you can inspect. For deeper analysis, the docs suggest sending the dashboard on to another tool.
features.replaces: Hand-writing SQL for a one-off question, exporting the result and building a chart in a spreadsheet.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Build a dashboard from the telemetry tables in our warehouse.

How does this month's rate of drive replacements per 1,000 deployed drives compare with the previous three months, split by drive model and by region? Add a filter for firmware version and a weekly view. Name the tables you used, and flag any model where the sample is too small to trust.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Connect the data you want to ask about. That can be a data warehouse such as BigQuery, Databricks or Snowflake, or another app you have connected to Claude.
  2. Ask in any chat, or go to the Artifacts tab and select Data.
  3. Say what you want to know, not only what to chart, and name the table or app if you know it.
  4. Open a chart's query to see how Claude got the number. If it is not counting what you meant, tell Claude what to change.
  5. Click Share when it is ready.

Example

Build a dashboard from the telemetry tables in our warehouse.

How does this month's rate of drive replacements per 1,000 deployed drives compare with the previous three months, split by drive model and by region? Add a filter for firmware version and a weekly view. Name the tables you used, and flag any model where the sample is too small to trust.

At work

  • In a review. Each chart shows its query and when its data was last refreshed, so a number can be checked on the spot.
  • Trusted definitions. Certified queries (beta) are queries your data team has approved. Charts built on them carry a badge.

Pitfalls

  • Without live sharing, a shared dashboard loads data with each viewer's own connections, so a viewer without access sees an error for that part.
  • Live sharing (beta) lets people in your organization see results from your connection, so check what a dashboard shows first.
  • Data does not refresh on a schedule. It refreshes when someone opens the dashboard and the data is due.
  • Editing a certified query removes its certification.
  • Claude Data is for paid plans, and on Enterprise plans the beta features are off by default.

features.title: Claude Design
features.summary: Claude Design is the artifact template for designs, interactive prototypes, one-pagers and other visual work, built by chatting with Claude and refined on a canvas with your design system.
features.when: Use it when you need to show what something should look like, such as an internal tool screen or a one-pager, before anyone writes production code. Hand the result to Claude Code when it is ready to become software.
features.replaces: Describing a UI in prose in a ticket, or waiting for a designer to mock up an internal tool.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Design an internal tool for our ops team to review and approve firmware rollout requests.

Layout: a queue on the left with status filters, and a detail pane on the right showing the target fleet, the risk checklist and Approve and Reject buttons.
Audience: on-call engineers on a laptop.
Show me two alternative layouts for the detail pane.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask Claude for a design in a conversation, or select Output > Design in the message box, or pick a Design template in the Artifacts tab.
  2. Describe the goal, the layout, the content and the audience. Attach screenshots or a codebase for context.
  3. Review what Claude generates on the canvas.
  4. Use chat for structural changes, inline comments for a specific element, and direct editing to drag, resize and align.
  5. Use the Export button, or click Share to choose who can open it.

Example

Design an internal tool for our ops team to review and approve firmware rollout requests.

Layout: a queue on the left with status filters, and a detail pane on the right showing the target fleet, the risk checklist and Approve and Reject buttons.
Audience: on-call engineers on a laptop.
Show me two alternative layouts for the detail pane.

At work

  • Internal tools. Agree on a screen with the people who will use it before building, then use Handoff to Claude Code so the implementation continues from the design instead of a screenshot.
  • Staying on brand. With a design system attached, Claude builds with your real components and checks its output against them. In Claude Code, /design-sync pulls in your design system.

Pitfalls

  • Claude Design does not have version history yet. Ask Claude to save the current state before trying a different direction.
  • Two or more people editing the same design at once is still basic and may not work reliably.
  • If inline comments are not picked up, paste the feedback into the chat.
  • Design system import is only as good as its source. A messy codebase shows up in the output.
  • The standalone version at claude.ai/design closes on December 14, 2026.

features.title: Claude Docs
features.summary: Claude Docs is a rich-text document, saved to your Claude account, that you, your teammates and Claude write and edit together in real time.
features.when: Ask for a doc when the output is a spec, status report or guide that will go through several rounds of edits and comments. Use file creation when you only need a Word or PDF file to send.
features.replaces: Drafting in chat, pasting into a document tool, then pasting sections back to Claude for each revision.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Turn the plan we just worked through into a design doc I can share with the team.

Readers are the storage platform engineers. Cover problem and goals, non-goals, proposed design with a diagram, rejected alternatives, rollout plan and open questions. Two to three pages. Leave a comment wherever you made an assumption I should confirm.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In any conversation, ask Claude for a doc. You can also start your request with /docs, or select Output then Docs from the message box.
  2. Answer the few questions Claude asks before it starts, then watch it draft on screen.
  3. Click into the doc and type to edit directly, or ask in the conversation for the next pass.
  4. Select text and leave a comment. Mention @Claude in a comment to ask for an edit at that spot.
  5. Click Share to add people, or Export for Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs.

Example

Turn the plan we just worked through into a design doc I can share with the team.

Readers are the storage platform engineers. Cover problem and goals, non-goals, proposed design with a diagram, rejected alternatives, rollout plan and open questions. Two to three pages. Leave a comment wherever you made an assumption I should confirm.

At work

  • Design docs and specs. The plan you worked out in chat becomes a shareable document.
  • From a coding session. In Claude Code you can ask Claude to turn the session into a spec, runbook or readout.
  • Review in place. Editors work on the same doc at the same time, and every change is attributed to the person or to Claude.

Pitfalls

  • There is no comment-only access level yet, only viewers and editors.
  • Deleting a doc is permanent. There is no trash, and it becomes unavailable to everyone you shared it with.
  • Charts and diagrams do not update on their own. Ask Claude to pull the latest data.
  • People you share a doc with must sign in to Claude.
  • Claude acts with the permissions of the person who asked, so it cannot edit a doc for someone with view access.

features.title: Claude Motion
features.summary: Claude Motion is the artifact template that turns your content into short animations, such as an explainer or an animated chart, built as code and exported as MP4.
features.when: Use it when a moving explanation will land better than a static slide, for example showing how a process flows or how a number changed. It is not for realistic footage.
features.replaces: Screen-recording a slide transition, or asking someone with video tools to animate a chart.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Make a 30-second animated explainer for our engineering all-hands showing how a write travels through our storage stack.

Scenes: client request arrives, write lands in the journal, data is acknowledged, background process moves it to its final location, replica catches up. Label each component, show the acknowledgement point clearly, and end on one line of text stating the durability guarantee. It will play on a projector without sound.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask Claude for an animation in any chat, or select Output in the message box and choose Motion, or select a Motion template in the Artifacts tab.
  2. Say who will watch it, where it will play and roughly how long it should be.
  3. Attach the report, data or images Claude should build from.
  4. Ask for changes such as "Slow down the second scene", or adjust the animation yourself in the editor.
  5. Click Export and choose MP4, or click Share.

Example

Make a 30-second animated explainer for our engineering all-hands showing how a write travels through our storage stack.

Scenes: client request arrives, write lands in the journal, data is acknowledged, background process moves it to its final location, replica catches up. Label each component, show the acknowledgement point clearly, and end on one line of text stating the durability guarantee. It will play on a projector without sound.

At work

  • Explaining a system. A short walkthrough of a data path or a failover sequence for onboarding or an all-hands.
  • Animated charts. The docs give an animated chart for a deck as a standard use.
  • Cheap revisions. Because each animation is code, you can change one word, number or timing and the rest stays as it was.

Pitfalls

  • Claude Motion is in beta on Team and Enterprise plans only, per the docs, and is off by default on Enterprise plans until an owner turns it on.
  • It does not use a video generation model, so it does not create realistic footage or people.
  • Animations start private to you. Sharing is a separate step.
  • Longer or more complex animations use more of your usage limit than a typical message.

features.title: Claude Sheets
features.summary: Claude Sheets is a spreadsheet built into Claude, where you and Claude edit the same cells and formulas stay visible in the cells.
features.when: Use it for a light, shared tracker, budget or model you build with Claude. When the file already lives in Excel or Google Sheets, or you need those apps' full features, use Claude for Excel or Claude for Google Workspace instead.
features.replaces: Asking Claude for a table, pasting it into a spreadsheet and rebuilding the formulas yourself.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Build a sheet to track the firmware qualification matrix.

One row per drive model, one column per firmware version, with a status dropdown (Not started, Running, Passed, Failed) in each cell. Add a summary tab that counts each status per firmware version using formulas, and conditional formatting that turns Failed cells red.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask Claude for a sheet in any chat, or go to the Artifacts tab and select the Sheets tile.
  2. Say what the sheet is for and what you want to track. Give Claude your numbers if you have them.
  3. Ask for changes such as "Add a column for budget remaining" or "Highlight anything that's overdue."
  4. Click Share to work on it with others, or export it as an .xlsx or CSV file.

Example

Build a sheet to track the firmware qualification matrix.

One row per drive model, one column per firmware version, with a status dropdown (Not started, Running, Passed, Failed) in each cell. Add a summary tab that counts each status per firmware version using formulas, and conditional formatting that turns Failed cells red.

At work

  • Trackers you can audit. Formulas stay in the cells, so you can check how each number was calculated, and each edit Claude makes is outlined as it lands.
  • Starting from an export. Import a CSV file, or import from Google Sheets or Excel, then ask Claude to add the columns and summaries you need.
  • Asking about numbers. Select cells and ask a question such as "Why is this total higher than last month?"

Pitfalls

  • Claude Sheets is in beta on paid plans, and on Enterprise plans it is off until an owner turns it on.
  • A sheet can hold up to 100,000 cells.
  • Not available yet: pivot tables, protected ranges, find and replace, multi-column sort, filter views and PDF export.
  • Excel macros, VBA, Power Query, DAX and print layout are not supported.
  • Sheets cannot pull live data from connected apps.
  • Restoring an earlier version from version history also removes edits made after it.
  • Mobile has basic read-only access.

features.title: Claude Slides
features.summary: Claude Slides is the artifact template for presentations, built from your notes, reports or the work already in your chat, that you can edit, present from Claude and export.
features.when: Use it when you need a deck from material you already have and expect to revise it with Claude. Use Claude for PowerPoint when the deck must live in an existing PowerPoint file or template.
features.replaces: Rebuilding the content of a document slide by slide in a presentation tool.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Make a deck from the incident review doc in this chat for Friday's operations review.

Audience: engineering managers who were not on the call. Eight slides at most: what happened, customer impact, timeline, root cause, what we fixed, what is still open, asks. One idea per slide.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask for a deck in any chat, or select Output in the message box and choose the Slides template, or pick it in the Artifacts tab.
  2. Give Claude the notes, report or chat content the deck should be built from.
  3. Edit any slide directly, or ask Claude to change it.
  4. Open the Present menu in the toolbar and select Present. Use the Right arrow key or Space for the next slide and Escape to end.
  5. Click Export for PowerPoint or PDF, or send the deck to Google Slides as an editable file.

Example

Make a deck from the incident review doc in this chat for Friday's operations review.

Audience: engineering managers who were not on the call. Eight slides at most: what happened, customer impact, timeline, root cause, what we fixed, what is still open, asks. One idea per slide.

At work

  • Doc to deck. You can ask Claude to turn a Claude Doc into a presentation, so the review deck starts from the design doc.
  • Presenting without exporting. Present directly from Claude, with number keys 1 to 9 jumping to a slide and F toggling full screen.
  • House style. Decks can use a design system so new work picks up your colors, fonts and components.

Pitfalls

  • Delete or Backspace on a slide thumbnail deletes that slide right away. Cmd+Z (Ctrl+Z on Windows) brings it back.
  • An object that is part of the slide's layout cannot be moved with the arrow keys. Ask Claude to move it.
  • Artifacts start private. Sharing is a separate step, and sharing settings cannot be changed in the mobile apps.
  • Artifacts need Cloud code execution and file creation turned on in Settings > Capabilities.

features.title: Claude Whiteboards
features.summary: Claude Whiteboards is a shared board where you talk, type or sketch and Claude organizes your ideas into diagrams, flows and groups.
features.when: Use a board before you know what the final version should be, such as laying out options for a decision or running a retro. Once the structure is settled, have Claude turn it into a doc or deck.
features.replaces: Dumping thoughts into a text file and then redrawing them by hand in a diagram tool.

docs.title: What are artifacts and how do I use them?

features.example:
Map this process on a whiteboard from start to finish: what happens when a customer array reports a failed drive.

Steps I know: alert fires, support case opens, on-call triages, replacement ships, field tech swaps the drive, rebuild completes. Put the steps in order, group them by owning team, and tell me what is missing between "replacement ships" and "rebuild completes".
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask Claude for a whiteboard in any chat, or go to the Artifacts tab and select the tile labeled Whiteboard.
  2. Describe what you want to work through, or select the microphone next to the send button and dictate a brain dump.
  3. Ask Claude to regroup the board by theme or turn it into a timeline.
  4. Drag across a region of the board to ask Claude about just that part.
  5. When the thinking is done, ask Claude to turn the board into a doc or deck.

Example

Map this process on a whiteboard from start to finish: what happens when a customer array reports a failed drive.

Steps I know: alert fires, support case opens, on-call triages, replacement ships, field tech swaps the drive, rebuild completes. Put the steps in order, group them by owning team, and tell me what is missing between "replacement ships" and "rebuild completes".

At work

  • Retros and planning. Everyone on the board works on it live and can rearrange what is there, and you can follow a teammate around the board.
  • Finding gaps in a process. Ask what is missing between two steps. Claude adds its suggestions to the board for you to check.
  • From sketch to document. A prompt such as "Turn this board into a project plan" converts the settled structure into a doc.

Pitfalls

  • Whiteboards is in beta on paid plans, and off by default on Enterprise plans until an owner turns it on.
  • Claude works from what is on the board and does not use context from your connected apps.
  • You can add pictures and videos, but you cannot import a board from a file. File export is PNG.
  • It is not available to organizations with HIPAA-ready configurations.

features.title: Create and edit files
features.summary: Claude can run code in a sandboxed computing environment to create and edit real files in a chat, including Excel, PowerPoint, Word and PDF.
features.when: Use it when you need a downloadable file or an analysis of an uploaded CSV, not text to paste somewhere. For a living document you will keep editing in Claude, use an artifact template instead.
features.replaces: Building the spreadsheet, chart or slide deck by hand from numbers Claude gave you in chat.

docs.title: Create and edit files with Claude

features.example:
Using the attached CSV of last quarter's on-call pages, create an Excel workbook with:
- a cleaned data sheet (one row per page, parsed timestamps, service, severity, time to acknowledge)
- a pivot-style summary by service and week, built with formulas rather than pasted values
- a chart of pages per week
Then write a one-page Word summary of the three noisiest alerts and what you would change about each.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Go to Settings > Capabilities and turn on Code execution and file creation (called Create and edit files in the updated Settings layout). On Team and Enterprise plans an owner controls this in Organization settings > Capabilities.
  2. Upload a data file such as a CSV, or describe what you need from scratch.
  3. Ask for a specific file type and describe the structure, content and formatting you want.
  4. Download the file from the conversation, or save it to Google Drive.

Example

Using the attached CSV of last quarter's on-call pages, create an Excel workbook with:
- a cleaned data sheet (one row per page, parsed timestamps, service, severity, time to acknowledge)
- a pivot-style summary by service and week, built with formulas rather than pasted values
- a chart of pages per week
Then write a one-page Word summary of the three noisiest alerts and what you would change about each.

At work

  • Reports from raw exports. Turn a Jira or monitoring CSV export into a workbook with working formulas and a chart.
  • Format conversion. Convert a document into a PowerPoint presentation, or extract the tables in a PDF into a spreadsheet.
  • Quick data science. Claude can write and run Python for analysis and produce visualizations as PNG files.

Pitfalls

  • The maximum file size is 30MB per file for both uploads and downloads.
  • Creating files uses more of your usage limit than normal chat.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans network access for the sandbox is off or restricted by default, so package installs beyond what is pre-installed may be limited.
  • Instructions hidden in external files or websites could trick Claude into leaking data from its context, so monitor what it does.
  • Review the output. You may need to refine it.

features.title: Agent SDK
features.summary: The Agent SDK is a Python and TypeScript library that gives your own program the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code.
features.when: Use it when you want to embed an agent in an application or service you operate, with code deciding what to do with each message, rather than shelling out to the CLI.
features.replaces: Writing your own tool-calling loop, file tools and permission handling around the API.
features.example:
import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage


async def main():
    async for message in query(
        prompt="Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix any issues you find.",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Glob"],
            permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        ),
    ):
        if isinstance(message, ResultMessage):
            print(f"Done: {message.subtype}")


asyncio.run(main())
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In a new folder, create a virtual environment and run pip install claude-agent-sdk. For TypeScript, run npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk.
  2. Get an API key from the Claude Console and run export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-api-key.
  3. Save the script below as agent.py next to a utils.py you want checked.
  4. Run python agent.py. The run ends with Done: success.

Example

import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage


async def main():
    async for message in query(
        prompt="Review utils.py for bugs that would cause crashes. Fix any issues you find.",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Glob"],
            permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        ),
    ):
        if isinstance(message, ResultMessage):
            print(f"Done: {message.subtype}")


asyncio.run(main())

At work
