  • Internal tooling. Put the agent behind a job or bot your team already uses, with your code filtering the message stream.
  • Same setup as your terminal. Skills, commands and memory load from the project's .claude/ and from ~/.claude/, and hooks, subagents, MCP and permissions are available as options.
  • Other languages. The docs suggest running the CLI as a subprocess with -p and --output-format json when you are not using Python or TypeScript.

Pitfalls

  • Authenticate with an API key or a supported cloud provider. Unless previously approved, Anthropic does not allow third-party developers to offer claude.ai login or rate limits in their products.
  • The SDK reads the key from the process environment and does not load .env files for you.
  • The quickstart lists Node.js 18.14+ or Python 3.10+ as prerequisites.
  • Both SDKs bundle a native Claude Code binary, but some installs get none, for example npm ci --omit=optional.
  • A product built on the SDK must keep its own branding and may not present itself as Claude Code.

features.title: Cloud scheduled tasks (routines)
features.summary: A cloud scheduled task, formerly called a routine, is a saved prompt with repositories and connectors that runs as a Claude Code cloud session on a schedule, an API call or a GitHub event.
features.when: Use one for unattended, repeatable work with a clear outcome that should run even when your laptop is closed. Use /loop for quick polling inside an open session.
features.replaces: Remembering to do the same triage, summary or cleanup every morning.
features.example: /schedule every weekday at 9:07am, summarize the pull requests merged to the replicator repo since the last run, flag any that changed the public API without touching docs/, and open a draft PR that updates the changelog
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In any session, run /schedule with a description, for example /schedule daily PR review at 9am. Claude asks about the schedule, repositories and prompt before saving.
  2. Or create one at claude.ai/code/routines with New task.
  3. Click Run now on the task's detail page to test it.
  4. Open a run from the History list to see what Claude did, review changes and create a pull request.

Example

/schedule every weekday at 9:07am, summarize the pull requests merged to the replicator repo since the last run, flag any that changed the public API without touching docs/, and open a draft PR that updates the changelog

At work

  • Backlog maintenance. A nightly run labels new issues, assigns owners and posts a summary, so the team starts with a groomed queue.
  • Alert triage. Your monitoring tool calls the task's API endpoint, and Claude correlates the stack trace with recent commits and opens a draft fix.
  • Docs drift. A weekly run scans merged PRs and opens update PRs for documentation that references changed APIs.

Pitfalls

  • Scheduled tasks are in research preview. Behavior, limits and the API surface may change.
  • Runs work from a fresh clone in the cloud and cannot see your local files.
  • The task runs autonomously, so the prompt must be self-contained and say what success looks like.
  • A task belongs to your individual account. Commits, pull requests and connector actions such as Slack messages appear as you.
  • All your connected connectors are included by default. Remove the ones the task does not need.
  • Schedules cannot run more often than once per hour, and a run set exactly on the hour can start several minutes late.

features.title: GitHub Actions
features.summary: Claude Code GitHub Actions is a GitHub Action that runs Claude Code in your repository's workflows, so an @claude mention can implement changes and push commits.
features.when: Use it when work should start from GitHub itself, such as a comment on an issue or a cron schedule, and you want to control the workflow file, triggers and model yourself.
features.replaces: Pulling an issue down to your laptop just to make a small, well-described change.
features.example:
name: Claude Code
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
  pull_request_review_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  claude:
    if: contains(github.event.comment.body, '@claude')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
      id-token: write
      actions: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 1
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Install the GitHub CLI and run gh auth login. You need admin access to the repository.
  2. Open claude in the repository and run /install-github-app. It installs the Claude GitHub App, saves an authentication secret, pushes a branch with the workflow files and opens GitHub with a pull request ready to create.
  3. Create and merge that pull request.
  4. Comment @claude fix the TypeError in the user dashboard component on an issue or PR. Claude replies in a comment and updates it as it works.

Example

.github/workflows/claude.yml, responding to mentions:

name: Claude Code
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
  pull_request_review_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  claude:
    if: contains(github.event.comment.body, '@claude')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
      issues: write
      id-token: write
      actions: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          fetch-depth: 1
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1
        with:
          anthropic_api_key: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}

At work

  • Issues to pull requests. A teammate with write access mentions @claude on a well-described issue and reviews the result.
  • Scheduled reports. With a prompt input the action runs on any event, including a cron schedule, for example a daily summary of commits and open issues.
  • Your own review job. Pass a skill such as /code-review:code-review --comment as the prompt to post inline review comments on each PR.

Pitfalls

  • /install-github-app works only with github.com repositories.
  • The triggering user must have write access, and bot actors are rejected unless listed in allowed_bots.
  • Each run uses GitHub Actions minutes and API tokens. Set --max-turns in claude_args and a workflow timeout.
  • Never commit API keys. Store them as GitHub Secrets.
  • With a plain-text prompt in automation mode, Claude has no shell or GitHub API access until you grant tools with --allowedTools.

features.title: Goals with /goal
features.summary: The /goal command sets a completion condition, and Claude keeps starting new turns until a separate model judges the condition met or impossible.
features.when: Use it for substantial work with a verifiable end state, such as a migration that is done when every call site compiles and the tests pass, instead of prompting "continue" after each turn.
features.replaces: Coming back to find Claude stopped with a progress summary while items were still open.

docs.title: Keep Claude working toward a goal

features.example: /goal every call site of legacy_retry() under pkg/ is migrated to retry.Do, go build ./... exits 0 and go test ./pkg/... passes, with no test file deleted, or stop after 20 turns
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In a session, run /goal all tests in test/auth pass and the lint step is clean. Setting a goal starts a turn immediately.
  2. Watch for the /goal active indicator, which shows how long the goal has been running.
  3. Run /goal with no arguments to see the condition, turns evaluated, token spend and the evaluator's latest reason.
  4. Run /goal clear to stop early.

Example

/goal every call site of legacy_retry() under pkg/ is migrated to retry.Do, go build ./... exits 0 and go test ./pkg/... passes, with no test file deleted, or stop after 20 turns

At work

  • Migrations. One measurable end state, a stated check and a constraint are what the docs recommend for a condition that holds up over many turns.
  • Long background runs. The best practices guide says a goal matters most there, because Claude sometimes ends a turn with a progress summary while items are still open.
  • Scripts. claude -p "/goal CHANGELOG.md has an entry for every PR merged this week" runs the loop to completion in one invocation.

Pitfalls

  • The evaluator judges the condition against what appears in the conversation. It does not run commands or read files itself, so phrase the condition as something Claude's output can demonstrate.
  • A goal does not change your permission mode. In Manual mode Claude still asks before tool calls, so use auto mode for unattended goals.
  • One goal can be active per session. /clear removes it.
  • Add a turn or time clause such as or stop after 20 turns to bound the run, and check token spend with /goal.
  • A turn that fails on an error you have to fix clears the goal.

features.title: Loops and in-session scheduling
features.summary: The /loop skill re-runs a prompt on an interval inside an open Claude Code session, and plain-language requests can set one-time reminders.
features.when: Use it to poll a deploy, babysit a pull request or check back on a long build during a session. For work that must run without your machine, use a cloud scheduled task.
features.replaces: Re-typing "is it done yet?" and refreshing a CI page.

docs.title: Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Code Desktop

features.example: /loop 10m check the CI run for my branch. If a job failed, pull its log, diagnose, and push a minimal fix. If review comments arrived, address each one. If everything is green and quiet, say so in one line.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Run /loop 5m check if the deployment finished and tell me what happened. Claude schedules the job and confirms the cadence and job ID.
  2. Leave out the interval, as in /loop check whether CI passed and address any review comments, and Claude picks a delay between one minute and one hour after each iteration.
  3. Set a reminder in plain language, for example remind me at 3pm to push the release branch.
  4. Stop a fixed-interval loop by asking Claude to cancel it. Stop a self-paced loop by pressing Esc while it waits.

Example

/loop 10m check the CI run for my branch. If a job failed, pull its log, diagnose, and push a minimal fix. If review comments arrived, address each one. If everything is green and quiet, say so in one line.

At work

  • Babysitting a PR. A bare /loop runs a built-in maintenance prompt that continues unfinished work and tends to the branch's pull request, including review comments, failed CI and merge conflicts.
  • Your own default. Put your instructions in .claude/loop.md and a bare /loop runs those instead.
  • Durable local schedules. The desktop app's scheduled tasks run on your machine while the app is open and the computer is awake.

Pitfalls

  • Tasks fire only while Claude Code is running and idle. Closing the terminal stops them, unless you send the session to the background first.
  • Recurring tasks expire 7 days after creation.
  • There is no catch-up for fires missed while Claude is busy.
  • A scheduled fire does not execute built-in commands such as /model, or skills marked disable-model-invocation: true.
  • Loops keep using tokens while you are not typing. /usage lists the heaviest ones.

features.title: Non-interactive mode
features.summary: Non-interactive mode runs Claude Code from a script or pipeline with claude -p, reading stdin and printing the result like any command-line tool.
features.when: Use it when a task should run inside a script, a CI job or a shell pipe rather than in a conversation you watch.
features.replaces: Opening a session to paste a log or diff and copying the answer back out.
features.example:
gh pr diff "$1" | claude -p \
  --append-system-prompt "You are a security engineer. Review for vulnerabilities." \
  --output-format json
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Run claude -p "What does the auth module do?" in a project.
  2. Pipe data in and redirect the answer out with cat build-error.txt | claude -p 'concisely explain the root cause of this build error' > output.txt.
  3. Add --output-format json to get a JSON object with result, session_id and total_cost_usd.
  4. Let it act by listing tools, for example --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit".
  5. Follow up on the same conversation with claude -p "Now focus on the database queries" --continue.

Example

Save as review.sh and run bash review.sh 123 to review pull request 123:

gh pr diff "$1" | claude -p \
  --append-system-prompt "You are a security engineer. Review for vulnerabilities." \
  --output-format json

At work

  • A project-specific linter. Pipe git diff main into claude -p from a build script and have it report issues as filename:line.
  • Log triage in a pipeline. Pipe the tail of a log in and write the explanation to a file your on-call notes can link to.
  • Structured extraction. --output-format json with --json-schema returns data matching your schema in structured_output, ready for jq.

Pitfalls

  • In a Manual mode -p run, a tool call that needs approval is denied unless something approves it. Pass --allowedTools or a --permission-mode.
  • Without --bare, a -p run loads the project's hooks and connects its .mcp.json servers with no trust dialog, even in a folder you never trusted.
  • --bare skips CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, plugins and MCP discovery, and it does not use your subscription login, so set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
  • Piped stdin is capped at 10MB. Reference a file path in the prompt for larger inputs.
  • Cap runs with --max-turns and --max-budget-usd. The cost figures are client-side estimates.

features.title: Auto memory
features.summary: Auto memory is a set of notes Claude Code writes for itself about your preferences, corrections and project context, and loads into later sessions.
features.when: Rely on it for things you would otherwise repeat as corrections, and use CLAUDE.md instead when you want to write the rule yourself and share it with the team.
features.replaces: Giving Claude the same correction in every new session.
features.example: remember that integration tests in this repo need the array simulator running on port 8443, and that I prefer table-driven tests with one assertion helper per file
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In a local session, ask Claude to remember something, for example remember that the API tests require a local Redis instance.
  2. Watch for a line such as "Saved 2 memories" in the interface.
  3. Run /memory to browse the memory files, open the auto memory folder, or switch auto memory on or off.
  4. Open ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md. The files are plain markdown that you can edit or delete at any time.

Example

remember that integration tests in this repo need the array simulator running on port 8443, and that I prefer table-driven tests with one assertion helper per file

At work

  • Fewer repeated corrections. Claude saves four kinds of notes, marked user, feedback, project and reference, so a correction you give once can carry into the next session.
  • Pointers to other systems. A reference note records where information lives outside the project, such as an issue tracker or dashboard.
  • Parallel checkouts. All worktrees and subdirectories of the same git repository share one memory directory, so a preference learned in one worktree applies in the others.

Pitfalls

  • Only the first 200 lines of MEMORY.md, or the first 25KB, load at the start of a conversation. Topic files are read on demand.
  • Auto memory is machine-local. It is not shared across machines or cloud environments.
  • Claude does not save something every session, and it skips anything it can derive from the codebase or that your CLAUDE.md already says.
  • Like CLAUDE.md, memory is context, not enforcement.
  • The main conversation's auto memory is not loaded into subagents, except forks.
  • To turn it off for one project, set "autoMemoryEnabled": false in that project's settings, or set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1.

features.title: CLAUDE.md project memory
features.summary: CLAUDE.md is a markdown file of standing instructions that Claude Code loads at the start of every session in a project.
features.when: Reach for it when you correct the same thing twice, or keep re-explaining a build command, convention or team decision that Claude cannot find by reading the repo.
features.replaces: Retyping test commands, conventions and team decisions at the top of each session.
features.example:
# Commands
- Build: make build
- Run one test file: pytest tests/unit/test_replication.py -q

# Conventions
- New code raises errors through pkg/errors helpers
- Never edit files under gen/, they are generated from proto/

# Decisions that are not in the repo
- Schema migrations need review from the storage platform team
- Link the Confluence design page in every PR description

# More
- Git workflow @docs/git-instructions.md
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In your repository, start claude and run /init. Claude analyzes the codebase and writes a starter CLAUDE.md, or suggests improvements to an existing one.
  2. Cut the file down to what Claude cannot learn from the code, such as the exact test and lint commands, team decisions and misleading patterns.
  3. Run /context all and check the file is listed under Memory files.
  4. Put personal notes for this project in CLAUDE.local.md (add it to .gitignore) and preferences for every project in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

Example

A short project file at ./CLAUDE.md:

# Commands
- Build: make build
- Run one test file: pytest tests/unit/test_replication.py -q

# Conventions
- New code raises errors through pkg/errors helpers
- Never edit files under gen/, they are generated from proto/

# Decisions that are not in the repo
- Schema migrations need review from the storage platform team
- Link the Confluence design page in every PR description

# More
- Git workflow @docs/git-instructions.md

At work

  • Onboarding. A new teammate's first session starts with the build commands and conventions already loaded, because the file is shared through version control.
  • Review feedback that sticks. When a code review catches something Claude should have known, add one line.
  • Scoped rules. Put rules for one area in .claude/rules/api.md with paths: frontmatter so they load only when Claude works on matching files.

Pitfalls

  • Claude treats CLAUDE.md as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action every time, use a PreToolUse hook.
  • Target under 200 lines per file. Longer files use more context and reduce adherence, and @path imports do not reduce that cost.
  • If two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily. /doctor prompt-audit reports outdated or conflicting instructions.

features.title: Monorepos and large codebases
features.summary: The large codebase guide shows how to scope Claude Code to the part of a big repository a task touches, using per-directory CLAUDE.md files, Read deny rules, sparse worktrees and code intelligence.
features.when: Apply it when a big repository fills the context window with instructions and file reads unrelated to your task, which costs tokens and degrades Claude's performance.
features.replaces: One giant root CLAUDE.md, and watching Claude wander through vendored and generated code.

docs.title: Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase

features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Decide where to start claude. From the repository root it can reach every file and loads the root CLAUDE.md. From a subdirectory it reaches that subtree and loads that directory's CLAUDE.md plus every ancestor's.
  2. Split instructions. Keep repository-wide rules in the root CLAUDE.md and put each subsystem's conventions in its own CLAUDE.md.
  3. Add Read deny rules for checked-in generated and vendored code, as in the example.
  4. Run /context all and check the list under Memory files to confirm which instruction files loaded.

Example

A .claude/settings.json that keeps Claude out of build output and vendored code and limits new worktrees to two packages:

{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Read(./**/dist/**/*)",
      "Read(./**/build/**/*)",
      "Read(./**/*.generated.*)",
      "Read(./**/vendor/**/*)"
    ]
  },
  "worktree": {
    "sparsePaths": [".claude", "packages/api", "packages/shared"]
  }
}

At work

  • Only the conventions you need. Starting from packages/api/ loads its rules and the root rules, with nothing from sibling packages in context.
  • Skip other teams' instructions. claudeMdExcludes in .claude/settings.local.json, for example "**/packages/web/**", stops those files from ever loading.
  • Cross-package changes. Grant a sibling directory with claude --add-dir ../shared, and plan first in plan mode, because the plan file is re-injected after each compaction.

Pitfalls

  • Project settings in .claude/settings.json are not inherited from parent directories the way CLAUDE.md files are.
  • Content searches already respect .gitignore, so deny rules are only needed for paths that are checked in.
  • End directory patterns with /**/* rather than /**, so Claude can still list the directory.
  • Relative Read patterns anchor at the session's working directory, not the repository root.
  • Include .claude in sparsePaths if you want the root settings and rules inside the worktree.
  • A directory added through the additionalDirectories setting never loads its CLAUDE.md, rules or skills.

features.title: Permission modes and auto mode
features.summary: A permission mode sets which actions Claude Code may take without asking you, from Manual review of every action to auto mode with a classifier.
features.when: Switch modes when the prompts no longer match the risk, for example Manual for sensitive work and auto mode for a long refactor whose direction you trust.
features.replaces: Approving the same harmless edits and commands one prompt at a time.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Look at the status bar under the prompt. It names the active mode, for example auto mode on or manual mode on.
  2. Press Shift+Tab to cycle. From auto the first press goes to Manual (default), then acceptEdits, then plan.
  3. Start a session in a chosen mode with claude --permission-mode acceptEdits.
  4. In VS Code, click the mode indicator at the bottom of the prompt box instead.

Example

Save this in ~/.claude/settings.json to make every terminal session on your machine start in Manual mode:

{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "default"
  }
}

At work

  • Code you are reviewing. acceptEdits lets Claude edit files and run common filesystem commands such as mkdir, mv and cp in your working directory, and you review afterwards with git diff.
  • Long tasks. In auto mode a separate classifier model reviews actions and blocks things such as curl | bash, force pushes, production deploys and git reset --hard.
  • CI. dontAsk denies anything that would prompt, so a pipeline runs only what you pre-approved with --allowedTools.

Pitfalls

  • The docs warn that auto mode reduces prompts but does not guarantee safety. Keep reviewing sensitive operations.
  • If the classifier blocks an action 3 times in a row or 20 times in total, auto mode pauses and prompting resumes.
  • defaultMode: "auto" has no effect in .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json. Put it in ~/.claude/settings.json.
  • Auto mode needs a supported model, and an organization can turn it off with permissions.disableAutoMode.
  • bypassPermissions is meant for isolated containers and VMs only.
  • Deny rules block in every mode, and explicit ask rules still prompt in auto mode.

features.title: Permission rules
features.summary: Permission rules are allow, ask and deny entries in settings files that decide which tool calls run, prompt or are blocked.
features.when: Add rules when a permission mode is too coarse, for example to pre-approve your test command or to keep Claude out of secrets files in every mode.
features.replaces: Clicking through the same approval prompt, and trusting a line in CLAUDE.md to keep Claude away from sensitive files.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Run /permissions to see every rule and the settings file it comes from.
  2. Add an allow rule for a command you approve constantly, such as Bash(npm run test *).
  3. Add a deny rule for a file Claude must not open, such as Read(./.env).
  4. Keep team rules in .claude/settings.json and commit it. Keep personal rules in .claude/settings.local.json or ~/.claude/settings.json.

Example

A shared .claude/settings.json:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(npm run lint)",
      "Bash(npm run test *)"
    ],
    "deny": [
      "Read(./.env)",
      "Read(./.env.*)",
      "Bash(git push *)"
    ]
  }
}

At work

  • Team baseline. Commit the rules so every clone gets the same pre-approved build and test commands.
  • Secrets. Claude Code also applies a Read deny rule, on a best-effort basis, to @file mentions and to the selection a connected IDE shares with Claude.
  • Less prompt fatigue. The bundled /fewer-permission-prompts skill scans your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP calls and adds an allowlist to the project settings.

Pitfalls

  • Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow. An allow rule cannot carve an exception out of a deny rule.
  • Put the * after the subcommand. Bash(git *) allows every git command, and without the space Bash(git diff*) also matches git diff-index.
  • A bare tool name in a deny rule, such as Bash, removes the whole tool.
  • A .claudeignore file has no effect. Move its entries into Read deny rules.
  • Read and Edit deny rules do not stop a script or subprocess that opens files itself. Use the sandbox for OS-level enforcement.
  • Rules are enforced by Claude Code, not the model, so wording in a prompt does not change them.

features.title: Plan mode
features.summary: Plan mode has Claude read the code and write a plan for a change, with edits blocked until you approve it.
features.when: Use it before a change that spans several files or where the approach is not obvious, instead of letting Claude start editing and correcting it afterwards.
features.replaces: Finding out halfway through a diff that Claude took the wrong approach.

docs.title: Use Claude Code in the cloud

features.example: /plan migrate the retry logic in pkg/replication from fixed sleeps to exponential backoff. List every call site, the order you would change them in, which tests cover each one, and what could break for callers. Do not add new dependencies.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In a session, press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows plan mode on, or prefix one prompt with /plan.
  2. Describe the change. Claude reads files, runs shell commands to explore and writes a plan without editing your source.
  3. Press Ctrl+G to open the proposed plan in your text editor and change it directly.
  4. Choose Yes, and use auto mode, Yes, manually approve edits, or No, keep planning and say what to change.

Example

/plan migrate the retry logic in pkg/replication from fixed sleeps to exponential backoff. List every call site, the order you would change them in, which tests cover each one, and what could break for callers. Do not add new dependencies.

At work

  • Design before code. Review the plan as you would a short design note, edit it, then approve. The costs guide recommends this for complex tasks because it prevents expensive rework when the first direction is wrong.
  • Plan locally, run elsewhere. Start with claude --permission-mode plan, save the agreed plan to the repo, push, then run claude --cloud "Execute the migration plan in docs/migration-plan.md".
  • Unfamiliar code. Explore a module and get a proposal without any risk of edits.

Pitfalls

  • Approving a plan exits plan mode and switches to the permission mode named in the option you picked. Press Shift+Tab or use /plan to plan again.
  • In an interactive terminal session started with bypass permissions available, plan mode's blocks are not enforced.
  • To start every terminal session in a project in plan mode, set defaultMode to plan in .claude/settings.json. The VS Code extension ignores project settings for this, so set claudeCode.initialPermissionMode there.

features.title: Sandboxed Bash
features.summary: The Bash sandbox is an operating-system boundary around the shell commands Claude runs, limiting which files they can write and which network hosts they can reach.
features.when: Turn it on when you want fewer approval prompts for shell commands without handing decisions to a classifier, or when commands should not touch anything outside the project.
features.replaces: Approving every build and test command by hand, or trusting that a script stays inside the repository.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In a session, run /sandbox. On macOS it works out of the box. On Linux and WSL2 the panel tells you if bubblewrap or socat is missing.
  2. On the Mode tab, choose auto-allow so sandboxed commands run without prompting, or regular permissions to keep the prompts.
  3. Ask Claude to run a build or test suite.
  4. The first time a command needs a new network domain, approve or deny it.

Example

Let sandboxed tools such as kubectl write to two extra locations:

{
  "sandbox": {
    "enabled": true,
    "filesystem": {
      "allowWrite": ["~/.kube", "/tmp/build"]
    }
  }
}

At work

  • Fewer prompts in Manual mode. The docs pair Manual mode with the sandbox in auto-allow mode as a way to iterate locally without a classifier.
  • Contain builds and tests. By default sandboxed commands can write only to the working directory, a per-user temp directory and directories you have added.
  • Control egress. Connections go through a local proxy that checks each host against your allowed domains, which start empty.

Pitfalls

  • The sandbox covers shell commands only. Claude's file tools, WebFetch, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.
  • It is off by default and runs on macOS, Linux and WSL2. On native Windows, commands run unsandboxed.
  • Reads are broad by default, including credential files such as ~/.ssh. Narrow them with filesystem.denyRead.
  • When a command fails in the sandbox, Claude may retry it unsandboxed, subject to your permission mode.
  • The docs call it risk reduction, not a complete isolation boundary. Allowing broad domains such as github.com can create paths for data exfiltration.
  • Deny rules still apply in auto-allow mode, and ask rules that name a command, such as Bash(git push *), still prompt.

features.title: Code intelligence plugins
features.summary: A code intelligence plugin connects Claude Code to a language server so Claude sees type errors after its edits and finds definitions and references by symbol.
features.when: Install one for a typed language in a large codebase, where text search returns too many candidates and you want errors caught before a build.
features.replaces: Waiting for the compiler to reveal a type error Claude introduced, and grep-then-read searches for a definition.
features.example: /plugin install gopls-lsp@claude-plugins-official
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Install the language server binary for your language. The docs table pairs each plugin with its binary, for example gopls for Go, clangd for C/C++, pyright-langserver for Python and rust-analyzer for Rust. Each plugin's README has the install command.
  2. Check the binary is on the PATH of the shell you start claude from, for example with which gopls.
  3. In a session, install the matching plugin with the command below.
  4. Ask Claude to introduce a type error in a file of that language and then fix it. A line such as Found N new diagnostic issues in M files (ctrl+o to expand) means the server started.

Example

/plugin install gopls-lsp@claude-plugins-official

At work

  • Errors caught at edit time. Each time Claude edits a file the server handles, it gets the server's errors and warnings, so a missing import shows up without running a compiler.
  • Navigation in big repositories. Claude gets a read-only LSP tool that looks up symbols through the server. The costs guide notes that one go-to-definition call can replace a grep followed by reading several candidate files.

Pitfalls

  • The plugin does not include the language server. Without the binary, /plugin shows Executable not found in $PATH on its Errors tab.
  • Code intelligence plugins work in terminal sessions. In cloud sessions Claude Code does not start plugin language servers.
  • The server starts the first time Claude edits a file with one of the plugin's extensions, not when the session opens.
  • If you installed the binary somewhere that is not on the PATH of the shell that launched claude, start a new session from a shell where it is.

features.title: Hooks
features.summary: Hooks are shell commands you configure that Claude Code runs at fixed points in its lifecycle, such as before a tool call or after a file edit.
features.when: Use a hook when something must happen every time, like formatting after edits or blocking changes to protected files, instead of asking Claude in a prompt and hoping it remembers.
features.replaces: Reminding Claude to run the formatter, and watching the terminal to see when it needs you.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open ~/.claude/settings.json (create it if needed) and add a hooks block like the one below. The notification command shown is for macOS.
  2. Type /hooks in a session and confirm your hooks appear under their events.
  3. Ask Claude to edit a JavaScript file, then open it to see the formatter ran.
  4. Switch away while Claude waits for permission. A desktop notification should appear.

Example

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write" }]
      }
    ],
    "Notification": [
      {
        "matcher": "",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "osascript -e 'display notification \"Claude Code needs your attention\" with title \"Claude Code\"'" }]
      }
    ]
  }
}

At work

  • Formatting without reminders. The PostToolUse hook formats every file Claude edits.
  • Protected paths. A PreToolUse script that exits with code 2 blocks edits to files such as .env or generated code, and its stderr message goes back to Claude.
  • A definition of done. A Stop hook running your typecheck with exit 2 on failure sends Claude back to work until it passes.

Pitfalls

  • Exit 0 from a PreToolUse hook does not approve the call. The normal permission flow still applies.
  • PostToolUse hooks cannot undo an action, because the tool has already run.
  • Stop hooks fire whenever Claude finishes responding, not only when a task is complete.
  • Matchers are case-sensitive and must match the tool name exactly.
  • The examples need jq, and hook scripts must be executable.
  • Hooks run with your full access, outside the Bash sandbox.
  • Put shared hooks in .claude/settings.json and personal ones in ~/.claude/settings.json.

features.title: MCP servers
features.summary: MCP servers give Claude Code tools beyond its built-in set, such as searching an issue tracker, querying a database or reading a monitoring dashboard.
features.when: Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into the chat from another tool, so Claude can read and act on that system directly.
features.replaces: Pasting ticket text, stack traces and query results into the prompt.

docs.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

features.example:
claude mcp add --transport http sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp
claude mcp list        # shows "! Needs authentication" until you sign in
claude                 # then run /mcp, select sentry, choose Authenticate
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In your terminal, not inside a session, run claude mcp add --transport http claude-code-docs https://code.claude.com/docs/mcp. This hosted docs server needs no sign-in.
  2. Run claude mcp list and look for Connected.
  3. Start claude and ask Use the claude-code-docs server to look up what MCP_TIMEOUT does.
  4. Remove it with claude mcp remove claude-code-docs when you are done.

Example

A hosted service with browser sign-in, using the docs' Sentry example:

claude mcp add --transport http sentry https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp
claude mcp list        # shows "! Needs authentication" until you sign in
claude                 # then run /mcp, select sentry, choose Authenticate

At work

  • Tickets to code. With an issue tracker connected, the docs example prompt is Add the feature described in JIRA issue ENG-4521 and create a PR on GitHub.
  • Connectors you already have. If you log in with a claude.ai account, connectors added at claude.ai/customize/connectors appear in /mcp automatically.
  • One config for the team. claude mcp add --scope project ... writes .mcp.json in the project root. Commit it, and teammates are prompted to approve the server.

Pitfalls

  • Verify that you trust a server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection.
  • By default a server is added at local scope, which is only you in this project. Use --scope user for all your projects. Changing scope means removing and re-adding.
  • Each connected server takes context space for its tool names and instructions. Remove or disable ones you do not use.
  • claude.ai connectors are not loaded when an API key or a third-party provider is the active authentication.
  • On Team and Enterprise plans, only admins can add connectors in claude.ai.

features.title: Plugins and marketplaces
features.summary: A plugin is a directory of skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit, usually from a marketplace.
features.when: Install a plugin to get a setup someone else built with one command, and make one when you want to hand several skills, hooks or servers to teammates as a versioned package.
features.replaces: Copying skill folders, hook scripts and server configs between repositories and teammates by hand.
features.example: /plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In a terminal session, run /plugin to browse the Discover tab, or run the install command below.
  2. Read the details pane. Will install lists the commands, agents, skills, hooks and servers the plugin adds.
  3. Choose a scope. User scope is for you in every project, project scope is for everyone in the repository, local scope is for you in this repository.
  4. Type / and look for the plugin's skills as /<plugin>:<skill>, for example /commit-commands:commit.

Example

/plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official

At work

  • One setup for the team. Install at project scope so the plugin entry lands in .claude/settings.json, which you commit.
  • An internal catalog. A marketplace is a repository with a .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file. Add yours with /plugin marketplace add followed by a GitHub owner/repo, a full git URL or a local path.
  • Housekeeping. The Installed tab lets you disable, update or uninstall, and claude plugin list prints the same list from your shell.

Pitfalls

  • An enabled plugin is part of every session. The names and descriptions of its skills and agents sit in context on every turn.
  • A plugin can run hooks and MCP servers, and what it runs, it runs as you. Read the details pane before installing.
  • Committing a project-scope entry turns the plugin on for collaborators but does not download it. Each runs claude plugin install <name>@<marketplace> --scope project once per clone.
  • Cloud sessions do not load plugins you installed on your own machine.
  • A plugin marketplace is not the Claude Marketplace website, which you cannot add with /plugin marketplace add.
  • Write git URLs with https://. A bare gitlab.example.com/your-group/your-marketplace.git is read as GitHub owner/repo shorthand and rejected.

features.title: Skills and custom commands
features.summary: A skill is a SKILL.md file of instructions that Claude Code loads when relevant or when you type its name as a slash command.
features.when: Create one when you keep pasting the same checklist or multi-step procedure into chat, or when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact.
features.replaces: Pasting the same PR template, review checklist or release steps into every session.
features.example:
---
description: Drafts a pull request description from the current branch. Use when the user asks for a PR description or a summary of their branch.
---

**Changes on this branch**

!`git diff main...HEAD --stat`

**Instructions**

Write a PR description for Jira issue $ARGUMENTS with these sections.
Summary in two sentences. What changed, as bullets by component.
How it was tested, with commands and results. Risks and rollback.
Do not invent test results. If no tests were run, say so.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Create a folder with mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/pr-description.
  2. Save the file below as ~/.claude/skills/pr-description/SKILL.md.
  3. In a git project, start claude and type /pr-description STOR-4821, or ask for a PR description and let Claude load the skill.
  4. To share it, move the folder to the project's .claude/skills/ and commit it.

Example

---
description: Drafts a pull request description from the current branch. Use when the user asks for a PR description or a summary of their branch.
---

**Changes on this branch**

!`git diff main...HEAD --stat`

**Instructions**

Write a PR description for Jira issue $ARGUMENTS with these sections.
Summary in two sentences. What changed, as bullets by component.
How it was tested, with commands and results. Risks and rollback.
Do not invent test results. If no tests were run, say so.

At work

  • Consistent write-ups. PR descriptions, incident summaries and release notes follow the same structure for everyone who clones the repo.
  • Risky procedures on your terms. Add disable-model-invocation: true to a deploy skill so only you can start it.
  • Cheaper context. A skill's body loads only when it is used, unlike CLAUDE.md, so long reference material costs almost nothing until needed.

Pitfalls

  • The description is how Claude decides to load a skill. Its combined text with when_to_use is cut at 1,536 characters in the listing.
  • If the frontmatter YAML is malformed, the skill loads with no metadata, so /name works but Claude cannot match it. Run with --debug to see the error.
  • Claude Code does not re-read the file on later turns, and after compaction it may keep only the start. Put key instructions first.
  • Personal skills in ~/.claude/skills/ do not load in cloud sessions.

features.title: Claude Code in Slack
features.summary: Claude Code in Slack turns an @Claude mention with a coding task into a Claude Code cloud session and reports progress back in the thread.
features.when: Use it to hand off a bug that is being discussed in a channel without leaving the conversation. Work in the web interface instead when you need to upload files or steer in real time.
features.replaces: Copying a bug report out of Slack into a new session and pasting the result back.
features.example: @Claude in the replicator repo, the nightly job fails with "snapshot lease expired". Stack trace: <paste the trace here>. Find the cause, fix it, add a regression test, and tell me what changed.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. A workspace administrator installs the Claude app from the Slack App Marketplace.
  2. Open the Claude app's App Home in Slack and click Connect Claude account.
  3. At claude.ai/code, connect GitHub and authenticate at least one repository with the same account.
  4. Pick a Routing Mode in the App Home, then invite the app to a channel with /invite @Claude.
  5. Mention @Claude with a coding request. When it finishes, use View session or Create PR.

Example

@Claude in the replicator repo, the nightly job fails with "snapshot lease expired". Stack trace: <paste the trace here>. Find the cause, fix it, add a regression test, and tell me what changed.

At work

  • Bug reports in a channel. Claude gathers context from your messages in the thread, picks a repository and starts a session, posting status updates as it goes.
  • Asynchronous starts. Kick off a task from Slack and get a direct message when it completes.

Pitfalls

  • The page marks this as an earlier version. It answers channel mentions only from Pro, Max and Ultra accounts, in a workspace that no organization has connected to Claude Tag. Team and Enterprise organizations are pointed to Claude Tag instead.
  • It works in channels only, not direct messages.
  • Repositories must be on GitHub, and each session can create one pull request.
  • Claude may follow directions from other messages in the conversation context, so use it only in trusted Slack conversations.
  • Claude reads your messages and its own, not your teammates'. Paste a colleague's error report into the message where you mention it.

features.title: Claude Code with Chrome
features.summary: Chrome integration connects Claude Code to the Claude in Chrome browser extension, so Claude can open pages, click, type and read console output from your session.
features.when: Use it when a change has to be checked in a real browser, or when a task lives in a web app you are already signed into and there is no API connector for it.
features.replaces: Switching to the browser to click through a flow and copying console errors back into the terminal.
features.example: I just updated the login form validation. Can you open localhost:3000, try submitting the form with invalid data, and check if the error messages appear correctly? Then check the console for any errors when the page loads.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Install the Claude in Chrome extension from the Chrome Web Store, and sign in to Claude Code with /login.
  2. Start with claude --chrome. The first launch shows a one-time dialog about site permissions.
  3. Ask for a browser task. Approve the prompt that starts with Claude in Chrome wants to.
  4. Run /chrome to check the connection. It is working when the panel shows "Status: Enabled" and "Extension: Installed".

Example

I just updated the login form validation. Can you open localhost:3000, try submitting the form with invalid data, and check if the error messages appear correctly? Then check the console for any errors when the page loads.

At work

  • Verify a UI change. Claude navigates to your local server, interacts with the form and reports what it observes.
  • Debug from console logs. Tell Claude which patterns to look for rather than asking for all console output, since logs can be verbose.
  • Web apps without connectors. Because Claude shares your browser's login state, it can work in apps such as Google Docs or Notion that you are signed into.

Pitfalls

  • The docs require a direct Anthropic plan and a /login sign-in. It is not available with an API key or through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry.
  • Claude can reach any site you are already signed into. Manage which sites it may use in the extension's settings.
  • At a login page or CAPTCHA, Claude pauses and asks you to handle it.
  • It works with Chrome, Edge and other Chromium-based browsers, and is not supported in WSL.
  • Selecting Enabled by default in /chrome increases context usage, because the browser tools are always loaded.

features.title: Computer use from the CLI
features.summary: Computer use lets Claude open apps, click, type and see your screen on macOS, so it can test native apps and drive tools that only have a graphical interface.
features.when: Reach for it only when nothing more precise applies, such as a native app, a simulator or a tool without a CLI or API. Claude prefers an MCP server, Bash or Chrome when one fits.
features.replaces: Clicking through a native app by hand to check a build, then describing what you saw.

docs.title: Let Claude use your computer from the CLI

features.example: Build the app target, launch it, and click through each tab to make sure nothing crashes. Screenshot any error states you find.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. In an interactive session on macOS, run /mcp, select computer-use and choose Enable. The setting persists per project.
  2. Ask for something that needs the GUI.
  3. Grant the two macOS permissions when prompted, Accessibility and Screen Recording, then select Try again.
  4. When Claude asks to control a specific app, choose Allow for this session or Deny.
  5. Press Esc at any time to stop.

Example

Build the app target, launch it, and click through each tab to make sure nothing crashes. Screenshot any error states you find.

At work

  • Validate a native build. Claude compiles, launches the app, clicks through the controls and reports what it finds.
  • Reproduce a layout bug. Claude resizes the window, reproduces the bug, screenshots it, patches the CSS and verifies the fix.
  • GUI-only tools. Design tools, hardware control panels or the iOS Simulator can be driven without a test harness.

Pitfalls

  • The page describes it as a research preview on macOS that requires a Pro, Max or Ultra plan and is not available on Team or Enterprise plans.
  • It needs an interactive session, so it does not work with -p.
  • Unlike the sandboxed Bash tool, it runs on your actual desktop with access to the apps you approve.
  • Only one session at a time can use your computer. The lock is released when that session exits.
  • Other visible apps are hidden while Claude works and restored when the turn ends.
  • Terminals and IDEs are click-only and browsers are view-only. Approving a terminal or Finder shows an extra warning because of what it grants.
  • It is the broadest and slowest way for Claude to interact with something.

features.title: Agent teams
features.summary: Agent teams are an experimental feature where one Claude Code session leads several teammate sessions that share a task list and message each other.
features.when: Try a team when parallel exploration adds real value and the workers need to challenge each other, such as a multi-angle review or competing debugging hypotheses. Use subagents when only the result matters.
features.replaces: Running several sessions by hand and carrying findings between them yourself.

docs.title: Orchestrate teams of Claude Code sessions

features.example: Create an agent team to review the changes on this branch before I open the PR. Spawn three teammates. One checks the retry and timeout logic for correctness, one looks for security problems in the new HTTP handlers, one checks test coverage for the changed files. Have them share findings and challenge anything they disagree on, then give me one ranked list.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Agent teams are off by default. Add "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "1" } to your settings.json and use an interactive session, since Claude spawns no teammates in -p runs.
  2. Describe the task and the teammates you want.
  3. In the agent panel below the prompt, select a teammate with the arrow keys and press Enter to message it directly.
  4. If the lead starts implementing on its own, tell it Wait for your teammates to complete their tasks before proceeding.

Example

Create an agent team to review the changes on this branch before I open the PR. Spawn three teammates. One checks the retry and timeout logic for correctness, one looks for security problems in the new HTTP handlers, one checks test coverage for the changed files. Have them share findings and challenge anything they disagree on, then give me one ranked list.

At work

  • Parallel code review. Each teammate takes one lens and they compare notes before you read one list.
  • Debugging with competing hypotheses. Teammates test different theories in parallel and converge faster.
  • Start small. The docs suggest research and review tasks first, with 3-5 teammates.

Pitfalls

  • The feature is experimental, with known limitations around session resumption, task coordination and shutdown.
  • Teams use significantly more tokens than one session. The costs guide puts it at roughly 7x when teammates run in plan mode.
  • Teammates do not inherit the lead's conversation history, so put task details in the spawn prompt.
  • Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites. Give each its own files.
  • With teams enabled, a subagent that Claude names launches as a teammate, so a team can form when you did not ask for one.

features.title: Agent view and background sessions
features.summary: Agent view, opened with claude agents, is one screen that lists your background Claude Code sessions and shows which are working, done or waiting for you.
features.when: Use it when you have several independent tasks to hand off and want to step in only when one needs you, instead of keeping a terminal open per task.
features.replaces: A row of terminal tabs that you cycle through to see whether anything is waiting.

docs.title: Manage multiple agents with agent view

features.example:
claude --bg "investigate why test_snapshot_restore is flaky and report the cause"
claude agents          # one screen for every session and its state
claude logs <id>       # print a session's recent output
claude stop <id>       # stop it
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Run claude agents in your project. If you have not trusted the folder yet, the workspace trust dialog appears first.
  2. Type a task and press Enter. A new background session starts and appears as a row. Each prompt you enter here starts another session.
  3. Select a row and press Space to peek at its latest output or question, and type a reply.
  4. Press Enter or → to attach to the full conversation, and ← on an empty prompt to detach.
  5. In a normal session, run /bg to send the conversation to the background.

Example

claude --bg "investigate why test_snapshot_restore is flaky and report the cause"
claude agents          # one screen for every session and its state
claude logs <id>       # print a session's recent output
claude stop <id>       # stop it

At work

  • Three tasks at once. Dispatch a bug fix, a pull request review and a flaky-test investigation as three rows, then check back when a row turns yellow for input or green for done.
  • Safe parallel edits. A dispatched session moves into its own git worktree under .claude/worktrees/ before it edits files.
  • Branch a line of thought. /fork copies the current conversation into a new background session while you keep working.

Pitfalls

  • Agent view is in research preview, so the interface and shortcuts may change.
  • Each session uses your subscription quota independently.
  • --bg cannot be combined with -p. The prompt is the positional argument.
  • A session you sent to the background with /bg keeps editing where it was already working, without a new worktree.
  • Sessions keep running when you close the terminal and survive sleep, but shutting the machine down stops them.

features.title: Cross-session messaging
features.summary: Cross-session messaging lets Claude deliver a plain-text message from one of your Claude Code sessions to another, on this machine, another machine or in the cloud.
features.when: Use it when one session learns something another needs mid-task, such as a breaking change or a finished migration, instead of copy-pasting between terminals.
features.replaces: Re-explaining a finding to a second session by hand.

docs.title: Message your other Claude Code sessions

features.example: Let @api-worker know the schema migration finished, that the new column is tenant_id, and that rebasing on main is safe now. Then ask it whether its integration tests still pass.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Open two sessions on the same machine and name each with /rename.
  2. In one session, run /list-agents to confirm messaging is available. If the command is not recognized, the session does not have the feature.
  3. Tell Claude what the other session should know. Type @ and the first letters of the session's name to pick the target.
  4. In the receiving session, look for a line such as › Message from @api-worker: Schema migration finished and press Ctrl+O to read the full text.

Example

Let @api-worker know the schema migration finished, that the new column is tenant_id, and that rebasing on main is safe now. Then ask it whether its integration tests still pass.

At work

  • Hand over a finding. When one session discovers a breaking change, Claude summarizes it for the session working on the affected area.
  • Coordinate parallel worktrees. Sessions working the same repository can tell each other what landed.
  • Status from long-running work. Ask a session running a migration or test suite to report back to the one you are watching.

Pitfalls

  • A message is text that one Claude writes to another. It never carries the sender's conversation history or files.
  • Messages on the same machine travel over a local per-session socket and never through Anthropic servers. Reaching sessions on other machines or in the cloud needs Remote Control with a claude.ai sign-in.
  • The receiving session applies its own inbound controls and can hold or drop a message. Set crossSessionInbound to refuse to stop a session receiving them.
  • Repeated messages are rate-limited per sender and at most 50 accepted messages are queued, so a loop between two sessions stops on its own.

features.title: Dynamic workflows
features.summary: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that Claude writes to run many subagents in the background and cross-check their results.
features.when: Use one when a job needs more agents than a single conversation can coordinate, such as a codebase-wide audit or a large migration, or when you want findings verified against each other.
features.replaces: Splitting a big audit or migration into dozens of prompts by hand and merging the answers yourself.

docs.title: Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows

features.example: use a workflow to audit every route handler under src/routes/ for missing authentication checks, and adversarially verify each finding before reporting it
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Run the bundled workflow /deep-research followed by a question. It needs the WebSearch tool.
  2. Select Yes when Claude Code asks whether to allow the workflow.
  3. Run /workflows to watch each phase and its agents. Press p to pause or resume and x to stop.
  4. For your own task, say use a workflow or include the keyword ultracode in the prompt.
  5. To reuse a run, press s in /workflows and save the script to .claude/workflows/ or ~/.claude/workflows/. It then runs as /<name>.

Example

use a workflow to audit every route handler under src/routes/ for missing authentication checks, and adversarially verify each finding before reporting it

At work

  • Audits. One agent per file, then independent agents check each finding, so you read a filtered list.
  • Migrations. Ask for each file to be migrated in its own isolated copy and verified.
  • Fix until green. Ask for a workflow that runs npx tsc --noEmit and keeps fixing errors until the check passes or two rounds in a row make no progress.

Pitfalls

  • The docs list dynamic workflows for all paid plans and API access. On Pro you turn them on in /config.
  • A run can use meaningfully more tokens than doing the task in conversation, and it counts toward your usage and rate limits. Try a small slice first.
  • A Large workflow warning appears above 25 agents or a projected 1.5 million tokens. It is advisory and does not pause the run.
  • A workflow takes no user input mid-run. Use separate workflows if you need sign-off between stages.
  • /effort ultracode makes Claude plan a workflow for every substantive task in the session. Turn it off with /effort ultracode off.

features.title: Subagents
features.summary: A subagent is a specialised worker that runs a side task in its own context window and returns only a summary to your conversation.
features.when: Delegate when a side task would flood your conversation with search results, logs or file contents you will not look at again, or when you keep spawning the same kind of worker.
features.replaces: Scrolling past pages of exploration output and re-typing the same reviewer instructions in each session.
features.example:
---
name: log-triage
description: Reads test and service logs and reports the failing step with evidence. Use proactively after a failed test run.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: haiku
---

You triage failures. Read the logs you are pointed at, find the first
real error, and report the failing step, the relevant log lines with
file paths, and the most likely cause. Do not edit files.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask Claude to create one, saying what it does, where to save it, which tools it may use and which model.
  2. Open the generated file and check the name, description, tools and model frontmatter.
  3. Delegate by name, Use the log-triage agent on the last test run, or type @ and pick the agent to guarantee it runs.
  4. Move the file to the project's .claude/agents/ directory and commit it to share it with the team.

Example

.claude/agents/log-triage.md:

---
name: log-triage
description: Reads test and service logs and reports the failing step with evidence. Use proactively after a failed test run.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: haiku
---

You triage failures. Read the logs you are pointed at, find the first
real error, and report the failing step, the relevant log lines with
file paths, and the most likely cause. Do not edit files.

At work

  • Log and test triage. Thousands of log lines stay in the subagent's context and you get a short report.
  • Independent review. A reviewer subagent starts fresh, so it has not seen the reasoning that produced the code.
  • A side task with full context. /subtask draft unit tests for the parser changes so far starts a fork that inherits the whole conversation and reports back when done.

Pitfalls

  • Each subagent sends its own requests, which count toward the same usage limits as your main conversation.
  • A non-fork subagent starts fresh. It gets its own system prompt and the task Claude writes for it, not your conversation.
  • Keep descriptions short. Claude Code warns at startup when the combined descriptions pass 15,000 tokens.
  • /rewind usually does not restore a subagent's edits. Use git for those.

features.title: Worktrees for parallel sessions
features.summary: The worktree flag starts Claude Code in a separate git worktree with its own files and branch, so parallel sessions do not edit the same checkout.
features.when: Use it when you want a second session to fix a bug or review a pull request while the first keeps building a feature in the same repository.
features.replaces: Stashing work, cloning the repository a second time, or waiting for one session to finish.
features.example:
# terminal 1: build the feature
claude --worktree feature-auth

# terminal 2: fix a bug at the same time, in its own checkout
claude --worktree fix-flaky-upload-test

# terminal 3: branch a worktree from pull request 1234 to review it
claude --worktree "#1234"
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. From a repository you have already opened with Claude Code, run claude --worktree feature-auth. The worktree is created under .claude/worktrees/feature-auth/ on a branch named worktree-feature-auth.
  2. Open another terminal and run the command again with a different name.
  3. Add .claude/worktrees/ to .gitignore.
  4. Add a .worktreeinclude file listing gitignored files such as .env so they are copied into each new worktree.
  5. When you exit, choose whether to keep or remove a worktree that has work in it.

Example

# terminal 1: build the feature
claude --worktree feature-auth

# terminal 2: fix a bug at the same time, in its own checkout
claude --worktree fix-flaky-upload-test

# terminal 3: branch a worktree from pull request 1234 to review it
claude --worktree "#1234"

At work

  • Feature and bug fix side by side. Neither session sees the other's half-finished edits.
  • Review without disturbing your branch. Passing #<number> or a pull request URL fetches that PR and branches the worktree from it.
  • Large mechanical changes. /batch <instruction> splits a change into 5 to 30 units and runs one background subagent per unit, each in its own worktree. A custom subagent gets the same isolation with isolation: worktree in its frontmatter.

Pitfalls

  • A worktree is a fresh checkout. Install dependencies there before running tests.
  • Removing a worktree deletes its directory and its branch, with all the work in them.
  • Worktrees branch from the repository's default branch unless worktree.baseRef is set to "head".
  • Non-interactive -p runs have no exit prompt, so their worktrees are not cleaned up. Remove them with git worktree remove.
  • Worktrees need a git repository, or WorktreeCreate hooks for another version control system.

features.title: Auto-fix for pull requests
features.summary: Auto-fix has a Claude Code cloud session watch a pull request and push a fix when a CI check fails or a reviewer leaves a comment.
features.when: Turn it on once a pull request is open and the remaining work is reacting to CI and review feedback, instead of checking the PR page yourself.
features.replaces: Polling a pull request for red checks and making small follow-up commits by hand.

docs.title: Use Claude Code in the cloud

features.example: /autofix-pr only fix lint and type errors
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Make sure the Claude GitHub App is installed on the repository and the gh CLI is set up.
  2. Check out the pull request's branch and run /autofix-pr in Claude Code. It detects the open PR with gh pr view and spawns a cloud session that watches it.
  3. Open the session at claude.ai/code to see what Claude does for each event.
  4. To stop, turn off Auto-fix in the pull request's ⋮ menu in the session's Changes card, or tell Claude to stop watching the PR.

Example

/autofix-pr only fix lint and type errors

At work

  • Red CI after a push. When a check fails, Claude investigates and pushes a fix if one is clear, and explains what it did in the session.
  • Review comments. Clear requests are fixed and pushed. For an ambiguous or architecturally significant comment, Claude asks you before acting.
  • From the desktop app. Turning on Auto-fix in a pull request's ⋮ menu has Claude fix failing checks for that session's PR.

Pitfalls

  • Auto-fix requires the Claude GitHub App on the repository, and /autofix-pr needs gh and access to cloud sessions.
  • Replies to review threads are posted from your GitHub account, labeled as coming from Claude Code.
  • If the repository has comment-triggered automation such as Atlantis or Terraform Cloud, Claude's replies can trigger it. The docs suggest disabling auto-fix where a PR comment can deploy infrastructure.
  • GitHub sends no event when the base branch advances and creates a merge conflict, so auto-fix cannot react to conflicts. Ask Claude to rebase.
  • By default the session is told to fix every CI failure and review comment. Pass a prompt to narrow that.

features.title: Code Review for pull requests
features.summary: Code Review is a managed service in which several Claude agents review each GitHub pull request, verify their findings and post them as inline comments.
features.when: Use it when every pull request in a repository should get an automatic first review without maintaining a workflow file. For a one-off pass on your own branch, run /code-review locally.
features.replaces: Human reviewers spending their first pass on logic errors and broken edge cases.
features.example:
# Review instructions

**What Important means here**

Reserve Important for findings that would break behavior, leak data,
or block a rollback. Style, naming, and refactoring suggestions are
Nit at most.

**Do not report**

- Anything CI already enforces: lint, formatting, type errors
- Generated files under `src/gen/` and any `*.lock` file

**Always check**

- New API routes have an integration test
- Log lines don't include email addresses, user IDs, or request bodies
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask an Owner of your Claude organization to turn the service on. Setup installs the Claude GitHub App and chooses repositories, a review level and when reviews run.
  2. On a pull request, comment @claude review. The command needs write access to the repository.
  3. Read the inline comments, ranked by severity, and the Claude Code Review check run.
  4. Commit a REVIEW.md at the repository root to tune what gets flagged.

Example

A REVIEW.md that recalibrates severity and cuts noise:

# Review instructions

**What Important means here**

Reserve Important for findings that would break behavior, leak data,
or block a rollback. Style, naming, and refactoring suggestions are
Nit at most.

**Do not report**

- Anything CI already enforces: lint, formatting, type errors
- Generated files under `src/gen/` and any `*.lock` file

**Always check**

- New API routes have an integration test
- Log lines don't include email addresses, user IDs, or request bodies

At work

  • A consistent first pass. Reviews focus on correctness by default, not formatting or missing test coverage, so people can spend their review on design.
  • Tuned per repository. An Owner can set Quick, Standard or Deep per repository, and REVIEW.md adds your own checks.

Pitfalls

  • The docs list it for Team and Enterprise plans, on GitHub repositories only, and not for organizations with Zero Data Retention.
  • A review never approves or blocks a pull request, and it reads the diff and surrounding code without building or running anything.
  • It can miss bugs. A review with no findings does not mean the code is error-free or secure.
  • REVIEW.md is read from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's own changes.

features.title: Local code review with /code-review
features.summary: The /code-review command has Claude review the changes on your branch, a pull request or a path for correctness bugs and report the findings in your session.
features.when: Run it before you open a pull request or before approving a teammate's, when you want a fresh reviewer that never saw the conversation that produced the code.
features.replaces: Rereading your own diff hoping to spot the bug, and pasting diffs into a chat window.
features.example: /code-review high main...my-feature
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. On a branch with changes, run /code-review. With no target it reviews your branch's commits ahead of its upstream plus your uncommitted changes.
  2. Keep working. In a terminal session the review runs as a background subagent and the findings arrive when it completes.
  3. Ask Claude to fix what it found, or rerun with --fix to have the findings applied to your working tree.
  4. Point it elsewhere with a target, such as /code-review 1234 for a pull request or /code-review src/auth for a path.

Example

/code-review high main...my-feature

At work

  • Before you push. Get a review of the branch from a subagent with its own context window before a person looks at it. /review is an alias.
  • Reviewing a teammate's PR. /code-review --comment 1234 posts the findings on the GitHub pull request as inline comments.
  • Security and cleanup passes. /security-review checks the branch diff for risks like injection and data exposure, and /simplify reviews for cleanup only.

Pitfalls

  • The review runs in your own session, so it counts toward your plan's usage or API billing.
  • A background review applies --fix edits outside your session's checkpoints. /rewind will not restore them, so use git.
  • The effort level trades coverage for confidence. low reports only the findings it is most confident in. From medium through max coverage broadens.
  • When you type no level, the review reuses the last level you typed, even from an earlier session.
  • It follows your CLAUDE.md but does not read REVIEW.md, which configures the managed Code Review service.
  • On GitLab, --comment posts through the glab CLI. Without it, findings print in the terminal.
  • /security-review needs an origin remote.

features.title: Ultrareview
features.summary: Ultrareview is a deep code review that runs a fleet of reviewer agents in a cloud sandbox and reports only findings it has independently reproduced and verified.
features.when: Run it before merging a substantial change when you want more confidence than a local review gives. Use the local /code-review for fast feedback while iterating.
features.replaces: A second and third manual read of a large, risky diff.
features.example: /code-review ultra 1234
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Sign in with a claude.ai account. If you use an API key only, run /login first.
  2. In a git repository, run /code-review ultra. With no arguments it reviews your branch against the default branch, including uncommitted and staged changes.
  3. Read the confirmation dialog. It shows the review scope, your remaining free runs and the estimated cost.
  4. Keep working. Use /tasks to see the running review. Verified findings arrive as a notification in your session.

Example

/code-review ultra 1234

At work

  • Pre-merge check on a big change. The docs position it for pre-merge confidence on substantial changes, at roughly 5 to 15 minutes per review.
  • Reviewing a pull request. Passing a PR number reviews that pull request on github.com and uploads nothing from your machine.
  • From CI or a script. claude ultrareview 1234 blocks until the review finishes and prints the findings to stdout.

Pitfalls

  • Ultrareview is a research preview. The feature, pricing and availability may change.
  • It bills against usage credits rather than your plan's included usage. The page lists three one-time free runs on Pro, Max and Ultra, then typically $5 to $25 per review depending on the size of the change.
  • It is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, or to organizations with Zero Data Retention. There, /code-review ultra runs a local review instead.
  • For a branch review, Claude Code bundles your repository state and uploads it to the cloud sandbox.
  • If you stop a review, no partial findings are returned, and a stopped run still uses a free run.
  • claude -p '/code-review ultra' exits without waiting for findings. Use the claude ultrareview subcommand in scripts.

features.title: Background commands and shell mode
features.summary: Background commands let a long-running shell command, such as a build, test run or dev server, keep going while Claude responds to new prompts.
features.when: Use it when a command takes minutes and you want to keep working in the same session instead of waiting or opening a second terminal.
features.replaces: Staring at a test run, or juggling a second terminal and pasting its output back in.
features.example: Start the dev server in the background, then run the integration suite in the background too. While they run, read ci/last-failure.log and propose a fix for the failing test. When the suite finishes, check its output and tell me which tests still fail.
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Ask Claude to run a slow command in the background, or press Ctrl+B while a Bash command is running to move it there. In tmux, press Ctrl+B twice.
  2. Keep prompting. The command gets a background task ID and writes its output to a file Claude can read.
  3. Run /tasks to see background work in the session and to stop an item.
  4. Try shell mode by typing ! npm test. The command runs directly and its output lands in the conversation.

Example

Start the dev server in the background, then run the integration suite in the background too. While they run, read ci/last-failure.log and propose a fix for the failing test. When the suite finishes, check its output and tell me which tests still fail.

At work

  • Long test suites and builds. Work on the next change while tests, make or a package install runs.
  • Dev servers. Keep a server up for the whole session while Claude edits and checks it.
  • Quick shell checks. After a ! command, Claude responds to the output automatically, so ! npm test gets you an explanation of the failures without a second prompt.

Pitfalls

  • Background tasks are cleaned up when Claude Code exits, and a resumed session does not restore background Bash tasks.
  • A command that reaches its timeout is moved to the background instead of being stopped, unless it starts with sleep.
  • In an unattended session, such as a -p run or a cloud session, a background command is stopped at its time limit.
  • Commands you type in shell mode usually run outside the sandbox, because the sandbox applies to commands Claude runs.

features.title: Built-in commands
features.summary: Built-in commands are slash-prefixed controls typed at the start of a message to manage a Claude Code session, such as /context, /diff, /model and /rewind.
features.when: Reach for a command when you want to change how the session runs or inspect its state, rather than describing that to Claude in a prompt.
features.replaces: Asking Claude in prose to do things the harness does directly, like showing the diff or clearing context.

docs.title: Use Claude Code in VS Code

features.example:
/init                      generate a starter CLAUDE.md
/plan fix the auth bug     enter plan mode with a task
/context                   see what is filling the context window
/diff                      review the working tree changes
/code-review               review the branch for correctness bugs
/security-review           check the branch diff for vulnerabilities
/clear oauth-migration     start fresh and name the session you leave
/resume oauth-migration    come back to it later
features.html:
Try it in a minute

  1. Type / in a session to see the commands available to you, then type letters to filter.
  2. Run /context to see what is filling the context window.
  3. Run /diff to review the changes in your working tree, including Claude's edits.
  4. Run /usage to see session cost, plan usage limits and activity stats.

Example

Commands across one working day:

/init                      generate a starter CLAUDE.md
/plan fix the auth bug     enter plan mode with a task
/context                   see what is filling the context window
/diff                      review the working tree changes
/code-review               review the branch for correctness bugs
/security-review           check the branch diff for vulnerabilities
/clear oauth-migration     start fresh and name the session you leave
/resume oauth-migration    come back to it later

At work

  • First session in a repo. /init, then /memory to refine the file, /mcp for servers and /permissions for approval rules.
  • Before you ship. /diff shows what changed, /code-review checks the diff for correctness bugs, and /security-review checks the branch for security vulnerabilities.
